Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe","uvicorn.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio*" OR Processes.parent_process="*autogen_studio*" OR Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio.web*") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","calc.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","bash.exe","wsl.exe","sh.exe","node.exe") OR Processes.process IN ("*-EncodedCommand*","*-enc *","*bash -c *","*cmd /c *","*sh -c *")) by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.parent_process, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe","uvicorn.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio*" OR Processes.parent_process="*autogen_studio*" OR Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio.web*") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","calc.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","bash.exe","wsl.exe","sh.exe","node.exe") OR Processes.process IN ("*-EncodedCommand*","*-enc *","*bash -c *","*cmd /c *","*sh -c *")) by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.parent_process, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Loopback WebSocket to AutoGen Studio MCP endpoint (/api/mcp/ws/ on :8081) from headless browser AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the AutoJack delivery vector: a headless browser owned by an AutoGen agent (Playwright/Chromium child of python.exe) opening a WebSocket to ws://127.0.0.1:8081/api/mcp/ws/ — the unauthenticated MCP control plane. Pairs the loopback flow with the autogenstudio parent chain so it doesn't fire on every chrome→localhost dev request. Rationale: Targets the article's exact exploit path: 'a webpage on the open internet, rendered by an AutoGen agent running on the same machine' opens a WebSocket to ws://localhost:8081/api/mcp/ws/. The two-stage join (Playwright/Chromium child of autogenstudio Python → loopback flow to :8081) constrains the hunt to actual agent-browsing contexts, not arbitrary chrome→localhost dev traffic.
ATT&CKT1199 T1071.001 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AutoGen Studio's own UI rendering pulling from its FastAPI on :8081 (legitimate /api/* HTTP requests, but the WebSocket /api/mcp/ws/ path is the actual signal — refine on RemoteUrl path if proxied)
  • Developer running an AutoGen tutorial where MultimodalWebSurfer legitimately exercises the local MCP server
  • Local dev port-forward where another service happens to bind 8081
  • End-to-end Playwright tests against a locally-served autogenstudio instance
  • Chrome DevTools opened against headless instance and connecting back to a local debug port that coincides with 8081
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the headless browser's parent chain to confirm it is a child of `python -m autogenstudio.web` (or similar). Capture the actual WebSocket URL via web-proxy or Sysmon DNS — if it contains `/api/mcp/ws/?server_params=`, treat as confirmed AutoJack delivery. Decode the base64 server_params blob; the JSON `command`+`args` fields are the attacker payload. Step 2 — Contain: Kill the autogenstudio Python service, block the external URL the agent was browsing (pivot from browser tab history under the python venv), and isolate the host. Step 3 — Hunt: For every device in the hit, run UC1 to confirm whether a child process was actually spawned; check git rev-parse on the autogenstudio install to see if it's pre-b047730; sweep DNS for the external lure domain across the fleet.
let AgentBrowsers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
         or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen_studio","MultimodalWebSurfer","playwright","fetch_webpage")
    | where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe","playwright.exe")
    | project AgentTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, BrowserProcessId = ProcessId, BrowserImage = FolderPath, AgentParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or RemoteUrl in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1")
| where RemotePort == 8081
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe","playwright.exe")
| join kind=inner AgentBrowsers on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.BrowserProcessId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, AgentParentCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let AgentBrowsers = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
         or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio","autogen_studio","MultimodalWebSurfer","playwright")
    | where TargetProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe")
    | project AgentTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, BrowserProcessId = TargetProcessId, AgentParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or DstHostname in~ ("localhost","127.0.0.1")
| where DstPortNumber == 8081
| join kind=inner AgentBrowsers on $left.DvcHostname == $right.DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (AgentTime .. AgentTime + 1h)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, AgentParentCmd
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:127.0.0.1 OR @DestinationIp:\:\:1 OR @DestinationHostname:(localhost OR LOCALHOST)) @DestinationPort:8081 @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\chromium.exe OR *\Chromium.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MsEdge.exe OR *\headless_shell.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\Node.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| (RemoteAddressIP4="127.0.0.1" OR RemoteAddressIP4="::1")
| RemotePort=8081
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|chromium|msedge|headless_shell|node|playwright)\.exe$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 | ParentBaseFileName=/^(python|pythonw|autogenstudio)\.exe$/i OR ParentCommandLine=/autogenstudio|autogen_studio|playwright/i | ImageFileName=/\\(chrome|chromium|msedge|headless_shell|node)\.exe$/i}, field=aid)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN ("127.0.0.1","::1","localhost") AND All_Traffic.dest_port=8081 AND All_Traffic.app IN ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe","playwright.exe") by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.user, All_Traffic.app, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | join type=inner src [ | tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe") by Processes.dest | rename Processes.dest as src | fields src ]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN ("127.0.0.1","::1","localhost") AND All_Traffic.dest_port=8081 AND All_Traffic.app IN ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe","playwright.exe") by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.user, All_Traffic.app, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | join type=inner src [ | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","autogenstudio.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*autogenstudio*") AND Processes.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","headless_shell.exe","node.exe") by Processes.dest | rename Processes.dest as src | fields src ]
Vulnerable AutoGen Studio MCP service exposed on loopback (pre-b047730 git build) AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory hunt for hosts running AutoGen Studio's MCP WebSocket surface (the AutoJack-affected component that was never shipped in PyPI). Detects the FastAPI/uvicorn process serving autogenstudio.web bound to :8081 so SOC can confirm exposure scope and force the b047730 patch. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'The affected MCP WebSocket surface was never included in a Python Package Index (PyPI) release' — meaning vulnerable hosts are those running autogenstudio from a git clone before commit b047730. This UC inventories which hosts are exposed; the loopback :8081 join confirms the MCP socket is actually listening. Aligns with the article's call-out that turning on auth in config.yaml does not close the hole.
ATT&CKT1133 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised AI research workstations running AutoGen Studio with the b047730 patch applied (verify by checking git rev-parse HEAD against the fix commit)
  • Developer sandboxes intentionally running AutoGen Studio for prototype experiments approved by AppSec
  • CI/CD runners exercising AutoGen Studio's test suite
  • Production AI orchestration that has migrated off the deprecated MCP WebSocket interface
Suppression filter
and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--version","--help","pip install") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath contains "\\site-packages\\pip\\")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: For each hit, identify the install path of autogenstudio (resolve the python process's cwd / venv site-packages) and run `git log -1` to confirm whether commit b047730 is present. If absent, host is vulnerable. Step 2 — Contain: Coordinate with the owner to either stop the autogenstudio.web process or pull the fix from upstream main. If the host has internet egress for the agent browsing tools and runs without containerisation, treat as high-priority — the AutoJack chain is one webpage away. Step 3 — Hunt: From the vulnerable host list, pivot into UC1/UC2 over the last 30 days to see whether the chain has already been exercised; review web-proxy logs for the autogenstudio user navigating to non-business external pages while the service was up.
let McpServers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio.web","autogen_studio.web","-m autogenstudio","autogenstudio ui","autogen_studio ui")
    | summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 5) by DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName;
McpServers
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where LocalPort == 8081 or RemotePort == 8081
    | where LocalIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1","0.0.0.0") or RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
    | summarize ConnCount = count(), DistinctSources = dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceId
) on DeviceId
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, Cmds, ConnCount, DistinctSources
| order by LastSeen desc
let McpServers = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe","autogenstudio.exe")
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("autogenstudio.web","autogen_studio.web","-m autogenstudio","autogenstudio ui")
    | summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Cmds = make_set(TargetProcessCommandLine, 5) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName;
McpServers
| join kind=leftouter (
    ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DstPortNumber == 8081
    | summarize ConnCount = count() by DvcHostname
) on DvcHostname
| project FirstSeen, LastSeen, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, Cmds, ConnCount
| order by LastSeen desc
title: AutoGen Studio MCP WebSocket Surface Running on Host (AutoJack exposure)
id: 4d2c1e9a-6b3f-4e22-90c8-7a1b5d44eef0
description: Hunts for hosts running the autogenstudio.web FastAPI surface — the AutoJack-affected MCP WebSocket endpoint that was never shipped in PyPI and remains exploitable on pre-b047730 git builds.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/

date: 2026/06/19
tags:

logsource:
  category: process_creation

detection:

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\(python|pythonw|uvicorn|autogenstudio)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/autogenstudio\.web|autogen_studio\.web|-m\s+autogenstudio|autogenstudio\s+ui|autogen_studio\s+ui/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count(), function=min(_time, as=FirstSeen), function=max(_time, as=LastSeen))

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Gentlemen ransomware uses multiple EDR killers to disable defenses

BleepingComputer
2026-06-18 9 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The Gentlemen ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) is actively developing and maintaining a suite of endpoint detection and response (EDR) killers to help affiliates evade detection in attacks. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Themida/Enigma packed binary with security-vendor masquerade name from user-writable path
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GentleKiller / HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller binary hash hit · [LLM] BYOVD vulnerable-driver service install impersonating Kaspersky/Valorant/Javelin/WatchDog · [LLM] Mass termination of 48-vendor EDR/AV process set within short window · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
GentleKiller / HexKiller / ThrottleBlood / HavocKiller binary hash hit AIInstallation High
Alerts on execution or file-write of any binary whose SHA1 matches the 20 ESET-published GentleKiller/HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller hashes tied to Gentlemen RaaS. These hashes were enumerated by ESET across at least 8 GentleKiller variants and three external EDR-killers. A hit means an in-scope ransomware-precursor binary touched the host and pre-encryption defense-disablement is imminent. Rationale: Uses the 20 SHA1 hashes attributed by ESET (the only researchers cited) to GentleKiller/HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller, covering both execution (ProcessEvents) and on-disk drop (FileEvents). The hash list is the article's most concrete IOC set and the only one that gives an unambiguous true-positive verdict.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reverse-engineer or malware analyst intentionally detonating sample on a lab host
  • SOC purple-team or BAS tool replaying the same hashes in a controlled test
  • Threat-intel ingestion pipeline writing the binary to a hashed quarantine path
  • Backup or forensic-imaging tools copying a previously-detected sample
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("malware-lab","sandbox-","-detonation") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AVAnalysis\", @"\Forensics\"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — confirm the device is a production endpoint, not the malware-analysis lab; pull full ProcessEvents/FileEvents tree for the matching SHA1 in the prior 60 minutes; identify the initiating user and parent binary (typical Gentlemen chain has the killer dropped after initial RDP / RMM intrusion). 2) CONTAIN — isolate the host via Defender or Falcon network containment; expire all cached credentials for the logged-on user; query EDR for any service stops on security products (Defender/CrowdStrike/SentinelOne) in the last 24h on this host. 3) HUNT — pivot on the parent process hash and the dropping account across the fleet; query for the same hashes anywhere in the estate (file-events) and for vulnerable-driver names (see UC2) since Gentlemen affiliates often pre-stage drivers on multiple hosts before encryption.

let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in~ (GentlemenSHA1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName=FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
ProcHits | union FileHits | order by Timestamp desc

BYOVD vulnerable-driver service install impersonating Kaspersky/Valorant/Javelin/WatchDog AIInstallation Medium
Hunts kernel-driver service creation where the service or ImagePath uses names GentleKiller variants impersonate — Kaspersky, Valorant (Riot), Javelin, WatchDog — but the driver file does NOT live under the legitimate vendor path. Catches the BYOVD step where Gentlemen registers a vulnerable driver under a security-product mask to obtain Ring 0. Rationale: Article explicitly lists Kaspersky / Valorant / Javelin / WatchDog as the four product names that GentleKiller variants impersonate, and ESET notes each variant ships a different vulnerable driver. Detecting the impersonated service-name + non-vendor path catches the BYOVD step regardless of which CVE driver the affiliate loads.
ATT&CKT1068 T1543.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Kaspersky AV reinstall from a non-standard custom installer path
  • Legit Valorant/Vanguard install on a corporate dev host (rare but happens on dual-use laptops)
  • Security-vendor IR tooling that registers a temporary kernel helper under a vendor-branded service name
  • Pen-test or BAS tool simulating a BYOVD install
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and RegistryValueData has_any (@"\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Riot Vanguard\"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — pull the InitiatingProcess (who registered the service) and the driver file SHA256; cross-reference the SHA256 against loldrivers.io to confirm it is a known vulnerable driver; verify the legit vendor product is/isn't actually installed via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory. 2) CONTAIN — stop and delete the rogue service (sc.exe delete <name>) before reboot; isolate the host; revoke the user session that wrote the registry value. 3) HUNT — pivot on the writing process across the fleet; search DeviceFileEvents for the driver SHA256 on every endpoint (Gentlemen pre-stages drivers across multiple hosts); check for any of the 20 hashes in UC1 on the same host in the prior 24h.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath" and RegistryValueData has_any ("kaspersky","valorant","vgk.sys","javelin","watchdog","wdog","wsdk"))
     or (RegistryKey has_any (@"\Services\kaspersky",@"\Services\valorant",@"\Services\vgk",@"\Services\javelin",@"\Services\watchdog",@"\Services\wdog") and RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath")
| where not (RegistryValueData has_any (@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
let ImpersonatedNames = dynamic(["kaspersky","valorant","vgk","javelin","watchdog","wdog","wsdk"]);
let LegitPaths = dynamic([@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\"]);
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Source == "Service Control Manager" and EventID == 7045
| extend ServiceName = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[0])
| extend ImagePath = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[1])
| extend ServiceType = tostring(parse_xml(EventData).EventData.Data[2])
| where ServiceType has "kernel" or ImagePath endswith ".sys"
| where tolower(ServiceName) has_any (ImpersonatedNames) or tolower(ImagePath) has_any (ImpersonatedNames)
| where not (ImagePath has_any (LegitPaths))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ImagePath, ServiceType, User
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gentlemen RaaS BYOVD Driver Service Install Impersonating Security Vendor

description: Detects creation of a kernel-mode service whose name or ImagePath impersonates Kaspersky, Riot Vanguard (Valorant/vgk), Javelin or WatchDog — the GentleKiller BYOVD masquerade — when the driver does not reside under the legitimate vendor path.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19

logsource:
  product: windows
  service: system
detection:
  selection_eid:
    Provider_Name: 'Service Control Manager'
    EventID: 7045
  selection_kernel:
    ServiceType|contains: 'kernel'
  selection_name:
    - ServiceName|contains:
        - 'kaspersky'
        - 'valorant'
        - 'vgk'
        - 'javelin'
        - 'watchdog'
        - 'wdog'
    - ImagePath|contains:
        - 'kaspersky'
        - 'valorant'
        - 'vgk.sys'
        - 'javelin'

  filter_legit:
    ImagePath|contains:
      - '\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\'

  condition: selection_eid and selection_kernel and selection_name and not filter_legit
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\\System\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\* OR *\\system\\currentcontrolset\\services\\*) (@Details:(*kaspersky* OR *Kaspersky* OR *KASPERSKY* OR *valorant* OR *Valorant* OR *VALORANT* OR *vgk.sys* OR *VGK.sys* OR *javelin* OR *Javelin* OR *JAVELIN* OR *watchdog* OR *WatchDog* OR *WATCHDOG*) OR @TargetObject:(*\\Services\\kaspersky* OR *\\Services\\Kaspersky* OR *\\Services\\valorant* OR *\\Services\\Valorant* OR *\\Services\\vgk* OR *\\Services\\Javelin* OR *\\Services\\WatchDog* OR *\\Services\\watchdog*)) -@Details:(*\\Program\ Files\\Kaspersky\ Lab\\* OR *\\Program\ Files\\Riot\ Vanguard\\* OR *\\Program\ Files\\Valorant\\*)

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Registry.registry_value_data) as ImagePath values(Registry.process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\System\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*\\ImagePath" (Registry.registry_value_data="*kaspersky*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*valorant*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*vgk*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*javelin*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*watchdog*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\kaspersky*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\valorant*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\vgk*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\javelin*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\watchdog*") by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_data | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | where NOT match(ImagePath, "(?i)\\\\Program Files\\\\(Kaspersky Lab|Riot Vanguard|Valorant)\\\\") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Registry.registry_value_data) as ImagePath values(Registry.process_name) as parent from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\System\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*\\ImagePath" (Registry.registry_value_data="*kaspersky*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*valorant*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*vgk*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*javelin*" OR Registry.registry_value_data="*watchdog*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\kaspersky*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\valorant*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\vgk*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\javelin*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Services\\watchdog*") by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_data | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | where NOT match(ImagePath, "(?i)\\\\Program Files\\\\(Kaspersky Lab|Riot Vanguard|Valorant)\\\\") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Themida/Enigma packed binary with security-vendor masquerade name from user-writable path AIDelivery Medium
Hunts process executions where the binary file name matches the security-vendor masks GentleKiller wears (Kaspersky, Valorant, Javelin, WatchDog), the binary runs from a user-writable directory (Temp, ProgramData, Public, Downloads), and the on-disk file is Themida/Enigma-packed. This catches GentleKiller variants where hash rotation has invalidated UC1 but the masquerade pattern is preserved. Rationale: Article calls out specifically that GentleKiller's 8 variants 'impersonate various legitimate security products, including Kaspersky, Valorant, Javelin, and WatchDog' and that the binaries are Themida/Enigma packed with stolen-but-invalid signatures. Anchoring on (impersonated name) ∧ (non-vendor path) survives hash rotation; signing-info anomaly is a useful tertiary signal.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer extracting a vendor installer to %TEMP% for analysis or repackaging
  • Custom IT-deployment script staging Kaspersky installer in C:\ProgramData\Kaspersky_install\
  • Gamer running Valorant from a non-default user-profile install
  • Security researcher detonating packed samples in a Downloads folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","vc_redist.x64.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$") and ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has_any ("Kaspersky","Riot Games")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — extract the SHA256, the ProcessVersionInfo block, and the signing status from DeviceFileEvents; check whether the legitimate vendor product is installed elsewhere on the host (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory) — if not, the masquerade is the whole point. 2) CONTAIN — kill the process, quarantine the binary, isolate the host if a kernel-driver service was also registered (correlate with UC2). 3) HUNT — search DeviceProcessEvents for the same binary by hash across the fleet; pivot on the dropping process to identify the upstream loader / initial-access vector; check FortiGate auth logs for the user given the article's note that Gentlemen targets FortiGate-configured environments.
let MasqNames = dynamic(["kaspersky","avp","avpui","valorant","vgc","vgk","javelin","watchdog","wdog"]);
let SuspectPaths = dynamic([@"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\PerfLogs\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\"]);
let LegitPaths = dynamic([@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Kaspersky Lab\"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend FNameLow = tolower(FileName)
| where FNameLow has_any (MasqNames)
| where FolderPath has_any (SuspectPaths)
| where not (FolderPath has_any (LegitPaths))
| extend SignerSuspect = (ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has_any ("Kaspersky","Riot Games","Microsoft")) or isempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1,
          ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName, ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SignerSuspect
| order by Timestamp desc
let MasqNames = dynamic(["kaspersky","avp","avpui","valorant","vgc","vgk","javelin","watchdog","wdog"]);
let SuspectPaths = dynamic([@"\Users\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Windows\Temp\", @"\PerfLogs\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Downloads\"]);
let LegitPaths = dynamic([@"\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"\Program Files\Riot Vanguard\", @"\Program Files\Valorant\"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend FNameLow = tolower(NewProcessName)
| where FNameLow has_any (MasqNames)
| where FNameLow has_any (SuspectPaths)
| where not (FNameLow has_any (LegitPaths))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mass termination of 48-vendor EDR/AV process set within short window AIInstallation High
Detects when 10+ distinct security-vendor processes (Microsoft Defender, CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, Palo Alto, Sophos, Trend Micro, ESET, Bitdefender, McAfee/Trellix, Kaspersky) terminate on a single host within a 5-minute window — the unmistakable signature of GentleKiller's kernel-mode process-kill loop targeting ~400 processes across ~48 vendors. Independent of which BYOVD driver or hash variant was used. Rationale: Article states GentleKiller 'targets more than 400 processes associated with approximately 48 security vendors' including the named vendor list. Threshold of 10 distinct security-vendor processes dying in 5 min is well above legitimate uninstall/upgrade noise (one product = ~3-5 procs) and matches the kernel-mode kill-loop signature shared across all 8 variants + HexKiller/ThrottleBlood/HavocKiller.
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bulk EDR migration day (uninstalling old agent + installing new) — usually scheduled & ticketed
  • SCCM/Intune deploying a corp-wide AV swap
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a stuck EDR with multiple service restarts
  • Disk imaging / golden-image refresh wiping security stack pre-recapture
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ (toscalar(DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory | where SoftwareName has_any ("CrowdStrike","SentinelOne","Defender for Endpoint") | where Timestamp between (ago(1h) .. now()) | summarize make_set(DeviceName))))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — verify against the change/maintenance calendar that no scheduled EDR swap or migration is running on the host; pull DeviceProcessEvents for the 30 minutes before the kill cluster to identify the parent that initiated termination; check for any UC1 hash or UC2 driver service in the same window. 2) CONTAIN — network-isolate immediately (ransomware encryption typically follows within minutes of EDR kill); force-reboot to reload the AV kernel components; do NOT trust the EDR's own response action — it may have been disabled. 3) HUNT — look for new local admin creations, SystemBC C2 beacons (article ties Gentlemen to a 1,570-host SystemBC botnet), shadow-copy deletion (vssadmin), and lateral RDP/SMB from this host to other endpoints; check FortiGate VPN auth logs for recent logons given the FortiBleed-credential targeting.
let VendorProcs = dynamic(["MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","SenseIR.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSFalconContainer.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SentinelServiceHost.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","cyserver.exe","cyveraservice.exe","CortexXDR.exe","SophosAgent.exe","SophosFS.exe","SophosHealth.exe","SophosClean.exe","tmlisten.exe","PccNTMon.exe","TmCCSF.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","eelam.exe","bdagent.exe","vsserv.exe","epsecurityservice.exe","masvc.exe","mcshield.exe","mfemms.exe","FrameworkService.exe","avp.exe","avpui.exe","kavfs.exe","klnagent.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "ProcessTerminated" or ActionType == "ProcessCreated"
| where FileName in~ (VendorProcs)
| summarize TerminatedProcs = make_set(FileName), VendorProcCount = dcount(FileName), FirstKill = min(Timestamp), LastKill = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where VendorProcCount >= 10
| order by FirstKill desc
let VendorProcs = dynamic(["MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","SenseIR.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSFalconContainer.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SentinelServiceHost.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","cyserver.exe","cyveraservice.exe","CortexXDR.exe","SophosAgent.exe","SophosFS.exe","SophosHealth.exe","SophosClean.exe","tmlisten.exe","PccNTMon.exe","TmCCSF.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","eelam.exe","bdagent.exe","vsserv.exe","epsecurityservice.exe","masvc.exe","mcshield.exe","mfemms.exe","FrameworkService.exe","avp.exe","avpui.exe","kavfs.exe","klnagent.exe"]);
SecurityEvent

| where VendorProcCount >= 10
| order by FirstKill desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process_name) as killed_processes dc(Processes.process_name) as VendorProcCount min(_time) as firstKill max(_time) as lastKill from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.action="terminated" (Processes.process_name IN ("MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","SenseIR.exe","SenseCncProxy.exe","MsSense.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSFalconContainer.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SentinelServiceHost.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","cyserver.exe","cyveraservice.exe","CortexXDR.exe","SophosAgent.exe","SophosFS.exe","SophosHealth.exe","SophosClean.exe","tmlisten.exe","PccNTMon.exe","TmCCSF.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","eelam.exe","bdagent.exe","vsserv.exe","epsecurityservice.exe","masvc.exe","mcshield.exe","mfemms.exe","FrameworkService.exe","avp.exe","avpui.exe","kavfs.exe","klnagent.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=5m | where VendorProcCount >= 10 | convert ctime(firstKill) ctime(lastKill)
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2022-42045", "CVE-2025-26125")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2022-42045", "CVE-2025-26125")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2022-42045", "CVE-2025-26125")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2022-42045", "CVE-2025-26125")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

let BadHashes = dynamic(["8AE6BD18B129061F63642531F1B684CF0383C75D", "BA914FE77B177B45799403B16DD14765C510A074", "D605994FC72A2BB59B5CFB1624A1B9170ECA73A2", "B0B912A3FD1C05D72080848EC4C92880004021A1", "5AA3124E5C4921E5EDFC60133B5D71DA21B07DA3", "7556AE58C215B8245A43F764F0676C7A8F0FDD1A", "331879F5EEC8892BBD896F90BDBB1BAD0BF63BD6", "F11AEBCCB9A86A7E2E653F90BAEC697F233C255F", "EF9CD06683159397F099CAA244E94E6EAAD96EBA", "711EF221526997039E804A18DB9647C91680BBE2", "68FEC379F2AE76C3D2CE913F7BE650CEA1D06990", "A11EE9CDC59E5CAA59AEFD27B30D104F3AD68E62", "96F0DBF52AED0AFD43E44500116B04B674F7358E", "2F86898528C6CAB3540C486A9BFAA0C029B73950", "9AD51AD97C01E97AB59214116740785E0F6320A8", "A19117175DBC9BA4D23B5DCE8415E299A2E32192", "12500F6C87CE62712A0ED6652C57468D15C14223", "D29670E684E40DDC89B47010C37CBC96737035B6", "56BEE9DF5833A637F5C54D5911DF98B0812FE643", "CF4D74DF17A91B4A36A2911B22AFEC5D8FA93A01", "EC296F9501AD71E430810CB5CDC38D954D4BA536", "7131B377E96016DC1911020C9F95B1B4D042D7B4", "82ED942A52CDCF120A8919730E00BA37619661A3", "F0537CBB773AE12100B36731E7C39F5A9D852B14", "1FA071303FB846308571E64727501FB98B1C2BE6", "A5CF917EC4A7DFBDFA43621398604805D860C718", "D4B19141102015D436321E6F26976E98183CFD27"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Gemini-MCP-tool @file exfiltration of sensitive paths (CVE-2026-0755)
Gemini-MCP-tool @file exfiltration of sensitive paths (CVE-2026-0755) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for Gemini CLI invoked under gemini-mcp-tool with @-prefixed references to sensitive local files (id_rsa, .env, /etc/passwd, .aws/credentials, path-traversal). In vulnerable versions 1.1.2–1.1.5 untrusted prompt content reached the @file parser and could exfiltrate arbitrary files outside the working directory. Rationale: GHSA-4h5r-5jm8-jxjm explicitly cites @/etc/passwd, @~/.ssh/id_rsa and @../../secret as the canonical exfil patterns. Pairing the sensitive-path token with a node/npx/gemini-mcp-tool parent yields a narrow, high-fidelity detection rooted directly in the advisory text — no external corroboration needed.
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.004 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers testing the patched 1.1.6+ build with legitimate @-references to files happening to contain 'env' in their name
  • Security teams verifying CVE-2026-0755 fix with intentional exfil probes (should be tagged in change-mgmt)
  • Documentation examples being copy-pasted into prompts that reference /etc/passwd
  • CTF/training environments using gemini-mcp-tool against intentionally-vulnerable hosts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","--test","vuln-verify","cve-2026-0755-test"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain. Run `npm ls -g gemini-mcp-tool` and per-project `npm ls gemini-mcp-tool` on the host to confirm version <1.1.6. Identify the prompt source — was it stdin, an IDE plugin, a chat UI, or a file? Untrusted prompt input is the injection vector. 2. CONTAIN: Force-upgrade to gemini-mcp-tool >=1.1.6 (`npm i -g gemini-mcp-tool@latest`). Rotate any credentials referenced in the @file paths (SSH keys, .env secrets, .aws/credentials). Snapshot host. 3. HUNT: Search egress to Gemini API (generativelanguage.googleapis.com) for POST bodies matching exfil'd file sizes from the same node PID. Pivot on user across chat-tool / IDE / web logs for prompt-injection patterns in the last 30d. Inventory all hosts running vulnerable versions via SBOM / TVM.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npx.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "gemini-mcp-tool"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("@/etc/passwd","@~/.ssh/","@/root/","@/proc/self/","@../","@./../","id_rsa",".aws\\credentials",".env")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "@"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\\node.exe","\\npx.exe") or CommandLine has "gemini-mcp-tool"
| where CommandLine has_any ("@/etc/passwd","@~/.ssh/","@/root/","@/proc/self/","@../","@./../","id_rsa",".aws\\credentials",".env")
| where CommandLine has "@"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gemini-MCP-tool @file exfiltration of sensitive paths (CVE-2026-0755)
id: 9c8d7e2a-1f4b-4a6c-8d3e-2b1f5e7a9c4d
description: Detects gemini-mcp-tool invoking Gemini CLI with @-prefixed references to sensitive files indicating CVE-2026-0755 exploitation
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4h5r-5jm8-jxjm
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1005
  - attack.t1552.004
  - attack.collection
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npx.exe'
  selection_sensitive:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '@/etc/passwd'
      - '@~/.ssh/'
      - '@/root/'
      - '@/proc/self/'
      - '@../'
      - 'id_rsa'
      - '.aws\credentials'
      - '.env'
  selection_at:
    CommandLine|contains: '@'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_sensitive and selection_at
falsepositives:
  - Developers legitimately referencing files with these names via @file
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\npx.exe OR *\\NPX.EXE) OR @CommandLine:(*gemini-mcp-tool* OR *Gemini-MCP-Tool*)) @CommandLine:(*id_rsa* OR *passwd* OR *credentials* OR *.env* OR */proc/self/* OR */root/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(node|npx)\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/gemini-mcp-tool/i
| regex("(@/etc/passwd|@~/\\.ssh/|@/root/|@/proc/self/|@\\.\\./|id_rsa|\\.aws\\\\credentials|\\.env)", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npx.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*gemini-mcp-tool*") AND (Processes.process="*@/etc/passwd*" OR Processes.process="*@~/.ssh/*" OR Processes.process="*@/root/*" OR Processes.process="*@/proc/self/*" OR Processes.process="*@../*" OR Processes.process="*id_rsa*" OR Processes.process="*.aws\\credentials*" OR Processes.process="*@*.env*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","npx.exe") OR Processes.parent_process="*gemini-mcp-tool*") AND (Processes.process="*@/etc/passwd*" OR Processes.process="*@~/.ssh/*" OR Processes.process="*@/root/*" OR Processes.process="*@/proc/self/*" OR Processes.process="*@../*" OR Processes.process="*id_rsa*" OR Processes.process="*.aws\\credentials*" OR Processes.process="*@*.env*") BY Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Windows cmd.exe metacharacter break-out via gemini-mcp-tool (CVE-2026-0755) AIExploitation High
On Windows, vulnerable gemini-mcp-tool (1.1.2–1.1.5) failed to quote cmd.exe arguments correctly, allowing untrusted prompt content containing shell metacharacters to break out of the argument and execute attacker commands. Hunts for cmd.exe spawned by node.exe with metacharacter+LOLBin payload signatures. Rationale: Advisory explicitly says: 'On Windows, unquoted cmd.exe metacharacters could break out into OS command injection.' Pairing node.exe→cmd.exe parent-child with metachar+LOLBin combinations (|powershell, &curl, &certutil, &bitsadmin) drives FPs down vs raw metacharacter matching, since legitimate npm scripts rarely chain cmd to download-capable LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • npm/yarn scripts using 'cmd /c ... && powershell.exe ...' intentionally for cross-shell pipelines
  • Electron / desktop Node apps invoking cmd.exe with curl for self-update
  • CI runners on developer hosts (Jenkins agents, GitHub Actions self-hosted) chaining cmd to powershell during builds
  • Vulnerability test harnesses replaying the CVE-2026-0755 PoC against patched hosts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run","yarn run","pnpm run","electron-builder","webpack"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Inspect the cmd.exe ChildCmd for the post-metachar payload — which LOLBin? what URL/hash? Confirm gemini-mcp-tool version on host via `npm ls -g gemini-mcp-tool`. Determine whether the prompt that triggered execution came from a trusted source or untrusted input (clipboard, file, web fetch, MCP client). 2. CONTAIN: Kill cmd.exe and child PIDs. Quarantine any downloaded payload. Upgrade gemini-mcp-tool to >=1.1.6. If a remote payload landed, isolate the host. 3. HUNT: Pivot on the injected payload URL/hash across the fleet. Check for persistence created within ±10min of the spawn (Run keys via DeviceRegistryEvents, scheduled tasks via DeviceEvents ActionType=ScheduledTaskCreated). Inventory all hosts with gemini-mcp-tool 1.1.2–1.1.5 via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory and prioritise patching.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("|powershell","&powershell","&&powershell","|curl","&curl","|certutil","&certutil","|bitsadmin","&bitsadmin","|mshta","&mshta","|wget","&wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("|powershell","&powershell","&&powershell","|curl","&curl","|certutil","&certutil","|bitsadmin","&bitsadmin","|mshta","&mshta","|wget","&wget")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-06-18 4 use cases 1 technique 4 kill-chain phases detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anomalous bulk export / cross-geo admin access to TinyPulse (WebMD) SaaS tenant · [LLM] First-time outbound to mega.nz file-sharing infrastructure (Shadowbyt3$ leak host) · [LLM] Inbound email referencing Shadowbyt3$ extortion / leak negotiation
Anomalous bulk export / cross-geo admin access to TinyPulse (WebMD) SaaS tenant AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the trusted-relationship abuse pattern Shadowbyt3$ used against Nintendo's TinyPulse tenant: bulk download/export or multi-country interactive sign-ins to the TinyPulse / WebMD Health Services employee-survey platform. Targets the SaaS audit telemetry where the actual collection occurred — Nintendo's endpoints saw nothing. Rationale: Pinned to the exact SaaS the article names (TinyPulse owned by WebMD Health Services). The article confirms Nintendo's endpoints were untouched, so the only place this attack is visible to Nintendo is in TinyPulse's SaaS audit feed and the SSO sign-in path used to reach it. Cross-geo / bulk-export signals match the kill-chain phase-1B detection hint verbatim.
ATT&CKT1199 T1213 T1530
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • HR / People-Ops admin running scheduled survey exports for analytics
  • Authorized data-migration off TinyPulse (Nintendo may now be doing exactly this post-breach)
  • Sales/CS user logging into WebMD/TinyPulse customer portal from a business trip — legitimate cross-geo
  • Service account performing API-driven analytics extracts that exceed the volumetric threshold
  • MSP / consultant tenant access from a different geography during a configured engagement
Suppression filter
| where AccountUpn !in~ ("hr-survey-admin@nintendo.com","peopleops-export@nintendo.com") and IPs !has_any ("<allowlisted-vendor-CIDR>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the user is an authorized TinyPulse admin (HR/People-Ops). Pull the matching IP geolocations, the user-agent string, and the TinyPulse audit-log line item for the export action. Compare against the user's normal sign-in baseline from SigninLogs over 90 days. 2) Contain: if the access is not pre-approved, force a password reset + revoke active sessions for the TinyPulse SSO app in Entra, and contact WebMD/TinyPulse support to revoke API tokens and pull tenant-side audit logs. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP across SigninLogs / CloudAppEvents for other SaaS apps (especially HR / payroll / benefits platforms — adjacent supply-chain targets), and check whether the same actor accessed any other shared third-party tenant in the last 30 days.
let TinyPulseApps = dynamic(["TinyPulse","tinypulse","WebMD","webmd","WebMD Health Services"]);
let BulkOps = dynamic(["Export","BulkDownload","MassDownload","DownloadFile","ExportToCsv","ExportData","DownloadReport"]);
let SignInAnomaly = AADSignInEventsBeta
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where Application has_any (TinyPulseApps) or ApplicationId has_any (TinyPulseApps)
  | where ErrorCode == 0
  | summarize SignInCount = count(),
              Countries = make_set(Country, 10),
              IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 25),
              FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
              by AccountUpn, Application
  | where array_length(Countries) > 2 or SignInCount > 200
  | extend Signal = "cross-geo or volumetric sign-in";
let BulkExport = CloudAppEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where Application has_any (TinyPulseApps)
  | where ActionType has_any (BulkOps)
     or (ActivityType has_any ("download","export","bulk") and isnotempty(ObjectName))
  | summarize EventCount = count(),
              Objects = make_set(ObjectName, 25),
              Countries = make_set(CountryCode, 10),
              IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
              FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
              by AccountDisplayName, Application, ActionType
  | extend Signal = "bulk export against TinyPulse";
SignInAnomaly
| union BulkExport
| order by LastSeen desc
let TinyPulseApps = dynamic(["TinyPulse","tinypulse","WebMD","webmd","WebMD Health Services"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where AppDisplayName has_any (TinyPulseApps) or ResourceDisplayName has_any (TinyPulseApps)
| where ResultType == 0
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| summarize SignInCount = count(),
            Countries = make_set(Country, 10),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 25),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| where array_length(Countries) > 2 or SignInCount > 200
| order by LastSeen desc
(source:azure.activeDirectory OR source:okta) (@properties.appDisplayName:(*TinyPulse* OR *tinypulse* OR *WebMD* OR *webmd*) OR @target.displayName:(*TinyPulse* OR *WebMD*)) @evt.outcome:success
#event_simpleName=IdpAuthenticationLog (TargetAppName=/tinypulse|webmd/i OR ApplicationName=/tinypulse|webmd/i) Result=Success
| groupBy([UserPrincipal, TargetAppName], function=[count(), count(field=CountryCode, distinct=true, as=CountryCount), collect([CountryCode, RemoteAddressIP4])])
| CountryCount > 2 OR _count > 200

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.src_ip) as src_ip dc(Authentication.src_ip) as ip_count dc(Authentication.src_country) as country_count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("*TinyPulse*","*tinypulse*","*WebMD*","*webmd*") Authentication.action="success" by Authentication.user Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where country_count > 2 OR ip_count > 10 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
First-time outbound to mega.nz file-sharing infrastructure (Shadowbyt3$ leak host) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects first-seen connections from any corporate device to mega.nz / mega.io / mega.co.nz — the file-sharing service Shadowbyt3$ uses to host their data-leak samples (named explicitly in the Nintendo breach post). Catches both (a) employees clicking the leak link to verify exposure and (b) any potential attacker reuse of mega.nz for exfil/staging from corporate infrastructure. Rationale: mega.nz is the exact host the article names — Shadowbyt3$ posted the leaked Nintendo employee data sample there. The first-seen anti-join eliminates noise from established personal-use patterns and surfaces the post-breach scenario (employees clicking the leak link, or attacker reuse against another corporate target). Pivots on RemoteUrl and DNS for redundancy.
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1567
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee personally using mega.nz for legitimate file storage on a BYOD or hybrid device
  • Security / IR team member fetching the leak sample for verification under approved IR
  • Marketing / creative team using mega.nz to receive large files from external vendors
  • Researcher or threat-intel analyst downloading public leak archives
  • Open-source project that hosts release binaries on mega.nz
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--headless","/silent","/quiet")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/device making the connection and check whether it was browser-initiated (likely a curious employee clicking the leak link) or process-initiated (potential automated exfil/staging). Pull the SHA256 of InitiatingProcessFileName and check it against known browsers. 2) Contain: if the process is non-browser or unsigned, isolate the device via Defender LiveResponse pending review; if browser, send the user a phishing-awareness reminder and confirm no leak-data was downloaded to local disk. 3) Hunt: query DeviceFileEvents for files written to disk from a mega.nz origin URL on the same host (FileOriginUrl has_any mega.nz) and look for archive files (.zip / .rar / .7z) written within the same window; pivot on the source IP for any other anonymous file-sharing destinations (anonfiles, gofile.io, pixeldrain).
let MegaPatterns = dynamic(["mega.nz","mega.io","mega.co.nz","g.api.mega.co.nz","userstorage.mega.co.nz"]);
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d))
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (MegaPatterns)
    | summarize by DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (MegaPatterns) or RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)\bmega\.(?:nz|io|co\.nz)\b"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DeviceId
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            ConnCount = count(),
            URLs = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10),
            IPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 10),
            Processes = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 5),
            CmdLines = make_set(InitiatingProcessCommandLine, 5)
            by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by FirstSeen desc
let MegaPatterns = dynamic(["mega.nz","mega.io","mega.co.nz","g.api.mega.co.nz"]);
let Baseline = (union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d)) | where RequestURL has_any (MegaPatterns) or DestinationHostName has_any (MegaPatterns) | summarize by SourceIP),
    (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated between (ago(90d) .. ago(7d)) | where Name has_any (MegaPatterns) | summarize by ClientIP=tostring(ClientIP))
  )
  | summarize by SourceIP;
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has_any (MegaPatterns) or DestinationHostName has_any (MegaPatterns)
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, Source="Proxy"),
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Name has_any (MegaPatterns)
    | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP=tostring(ClientIP), RequestURL=Name, Source="DNS")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on SourceIP
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), URLs=make_set(RequestURL, 10), Bytes=sum(coalesce(SentBytes,0)) by SourceIP, SourceUserName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Inbound email referencing Shadowbyt3$ extortion / leak negotiation AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on inbound email mentioning the Shadowbyt3$ threat actor name, ransom amount, or known leak-site language combined with mega.nz URLs — the exact extortion-contact pattern the article describes (48-hour negotiation window, $2M demand). Catches the initial extortion approach to Nintendo and any subsequent victim outreach by the same actor. Rationale: Shadowbyt3$ is the named actor; '48 hours', '$2 million', 'extortion as a service', and 'Deleted Permanently' are direct quotes from the article's ransom note. The mega.nz URL join confirms it's the same leak-distribution pattern. Very low FP risk because the actor name is unique.
ATT&CKT1657 T1486
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR / threat-intel team forwarding the BleepingComputer article internally for awareness
  • Vendor security-bulletin / SOC newsletter referencing the Nintendo breach
  • Legitimate inbound contact from journalists writing follow-up coverage
  • Phishing simulation that intentionally mimics extortion language for training
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !endswith "nintendo.com" and not (SenderFromAddress has_any ("@bleepingcomputer.com","@krebsonsecurity.com","securityalerts@"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the message, capture headers (especially Authentication-Results and Return-Path), verify the sender domain, and check whether the body contains a contact channel (Tox ID, qTox, Session, onion address, mega.nz link). Confirm whether the message reached an executive, legal, or comms inbox — those are the actor's typical targets. 2) Contain: quarantine the message tenant-wide via M365 Threat Explorer / soft-delete; alert legal + executive protection + comms before any reply is sent; do NOT engage with the threat actor. 3) Hunt: search EmailEvents for other inbound messages from the same SenderFromDomain or with the same mega.nz URL across the past 90 days; check whether any third-party HR/engagement SaaS (BambooHR, Culture Amp, Lattice, Officevibe) shows similar bulk-export or anomalous-geo sign-in activity — Shadowbyt3$ telegraphed 'more victims' so adjacent SaaS pivots are likely.
let ExtortionKeywords = dynamic(["Shadowbyt3","shadowbyt3","ShadowByt3$","shadow byt3"]);
let RansomLanguage = dynamic(["48 hours","48-hour","$2 million","2,000,000","extortion as a service","Deleted Permanently","leak site","data leak"]);
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where Subject has_any (ExtortionKeywords)
    or Subject has_any (RansomLanguage)
| join kind=leftouter (
    EmailUrlInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where Url has_any ("mega.nz","mega.io","mega.co.nz")
    | project NetworkMessageId, LeakUrl=Url
  ) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
          RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation,
          LeakUrl, ThreatTypes
| order by Timestamp desc
let ExtortionKeywords = dynamic(["Shadowbyt3","shadowbyt3","ShadowByt3"]);
let RansomLanguage = dynamic(["48 hours","$2 million","2,000,000","extortion as a service","Deleted Permanently","data leak"]);
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
| where Subject has_any (ExtortionKeywords) or Subject has_any (RansomLanguage)
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, Subject, Sender=tostring(Sender), Recipients=tostring(Recipients), MessageId=tostring(InternetMessageId)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
