Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Close Encounters of the Human Kind
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Talos top-prevalence malware hash sweep — VID001.exe coinminer + f_000cd7.html (week of 2026-06-18) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Talos top-prevalence malware hash sweep — VID001.exe coinminer + f_000cd7.html (week of 2026-06-18) AIInstallation High
Hunts for execution or file-write activity matching the two complete SHA256 hashes Talos identified as most prevalent in their telemetry this week: a Win.Worm.Coinminer dropper observed as VID001.exe and a malicious HTML payload observed as f_000cd7.html (W32.C0AD494457-95.SBX.TG). Pure hash-IOC sweep — the article gives no behavioural context to pivot on. Rationale: Article is a Talos weekly newsletter — bulk is commentary / headlines with no IOCs. The only article-specific detectable content is the 'Most prevalent malware files from Talos telemetry over the past week' block, which lists two complete SHA256 + MD5 pairs (the third is truncated and unusable). Hashes are concrete, high-fidelity strings directly from the article. Filename hints (VID001.exe, f_000cd7.html) added to SPL/Sigma as supplemental selectors. No web corroboration performed — these are Talos's own first-party telemetry hashes and there's no campaign context to enrich.
ATT&CKT1496 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst workstations intentionally detonating samples (researcher sandbox VMs)
  • VirusTotal / threat-intel platform API workers caching the sample locally
  • SOC purple-team exercises replaying Talos prevalence-list IOCs to validate detection coverage
  • Endpoint backup/EDR quarantine restore operations re-materialising the file on disk
  • Pre-existing dormant infection from prior week being newly flagged as the hash is added to the watchlist
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "analyst" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab"
| join kind=leftanti (DeviceInfo | where MachineGroup has_any ("Threat Research", "Malware Analysis", "Sandbox")) on DeviceId
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full process tree around the hit — parent process, command line, write origin (FileOriginUrl on DeviceFileEvents). Confirm device is production (not analyst/sandbox) via DeviceInfo.DeviceCategory and machine group. Check Talos reputation page links and pivot the SHA256 in VT for current verdict. 2. Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response / Falcon RTR if execution is confirmed (not just a stale file on disk). Kill the running process, quarantine the file, capture memory if coinminer behaviour suspected (high CPU, outbound to mining pools). 3. Hunt: pivot on the parent process / download URL and SHA256 of the dropper across the fleet to find sibling infections; query DeviceNetworkEvents for the host's outbound traffic in the hour around the file write for stratum+tcp:// mining-pool destinations (T1496) or unfamiliar C2 beacons; check DeviceRegistryEvents for Run-key persistence written by the same InitiatingProcessId.
let TalosTopHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe"]);
let ProcessHits = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where SHA256 in~ (TalosTopHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in~ (TalosTopHashes)
    | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceProcessEvents", DeviceName, AccountName,
              FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine,
              ParentFileName=InitiatingProcessFileName,
              ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let FileHits = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where SHA256 in~ (TalosTopHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in~ (TalosTopHashes)
    | project Timestamp, Source="DeviceFileEvents", DeviceName,
              AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
              ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              ParentFileName=InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
              ParentCmd="";
union ProcessHits, FileHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let TalosTopHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "c0ad494457dcd9e964378760fb6aca86a23622045bca851d8f3ab49ec33978fe"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (TalosTopHashes)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Crawl4AI /crawl endpoint POST with Chromium launcher-switch payload in body (GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44)

Crawl4AI /crawl endpoint POST with Chromium launcher-switch payload in body (GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44) AIDelivery High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests targeting Crawl4AI's /crawl, /crawl/stream, /crawl/job endpoints whose body or query string carries Chromium subprocess-launcher override switches (--utility-cmd-prefix, --renderer-cmd-prefix, --gpu-launcher, --browser-subprocess-path) and/or --no-zygote. This is the literal exploit shape for the unauthenticated RCE in pip:crawl4ai <= 0.8.9 — only WAF/reverse-proxy or API-gateway logs that capture the request body will see the payload. Rationale: Pivots on the three vulnerable endpoints named verbatim in the advisory (/crawl, /crawl/stream, /crawl/job) AND the exact Chromium switch list called out in the Summary (--utility-cmd-prefix, --renderer-cmd-prefix, --gpu-launcher, --browser-subprocess-path) plus --no-zygote, which the advisory explicitly identifies as the attack enabler. Co-occurrence of the endpoint and any one of these switches is near-zero in legitimate traffic — the patched 0.9.0 hard-rejects any request body containing extra_args, so even trusted callers do not transmit them over the wire.
ATT&CKT1190 T1659 T1203
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vuln scanners (Nuclei, Tenable, Qualys) replaying the public PoC against patched 0.9.0 hosts
  • Red team / pentest engagements probing exposed Crawl4AI Docker hosts
  • Crawl4AI Docker upgrade validation traffic from CI/CD pipelines
  • Trusted in-process SDK callers were never supposed to traverse the WAF — anything that does is anomalous
  • Security researchers fuzzing the advisory's PoC from research VPC ranges
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nuclei", "Nessus", "Qualys", "Tenable"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — Pull the full request body from WAF/proxy. Confirm it is a POST to /crawl* and the JSON payload literally contains browser_config.extra_args with one of the four launcher-switch keys. Identify the responding Crawl4AI host: get the running crawl4ai package version (pip show crawl4ai or docker image tag). If <= 0.8.9, treat as confirmed exploit attempt. 2. CONTAIN — Block source IP at the WAF. If version <= 0.8.9 AND a HTTP 200 was returned, isolate the container, snapshot it for forensics, and rotate every secret, token, and mounted credential reachable from the container's runtime user. Patch to 0.9.0 immediately or set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN and front the API with auth. 3. HUNT — On the container host hunt DeviceProcessEvents/auditd for chromium processes with --no-zygote co-occurring with any launcher-prefix switch (see UC #2), then walk child processes for shells, curl/wget, nc, base64 piping, and outbound connections to non-Chromium-update destinations.

| where RemotePort in (80, 8000, 8080, 11235, 443, 8443)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/crawl", "/crawl/stream", "/crawl/job")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--utility-cmd-prefix", "--renderer-cmd-prefix", "--gpu-launcher", "--browser-subprocess-path", "--no-zygote", "extra_args")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc

Chromium process invoked with --no-zygote AND subprocess-launcher override flag co-occurrence (Crawl4AI RCE) AIExploitation High
High-fidelity behavioural detection for the exploit primitive in GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44. The vulnerability turns into RCE only when a Chromium process is launched with --no-zygote (disables the sandbox-forking zygote) simultaneously with one of the four subprocess-launcher overrides (--utility-cmd-prefix, --renderer-cmd-prefix, --gpu-launcher, --browser-subprocess-path). That tuple is pathognomonic — legitimate Chromium use cases for these flags are limited to Chromium build/test farms, not production crawler containers. Rationale: The advisory's Summary names the exact switch set verbatim: '--utility-cmd-prefix, --renderer-cmd-prefix, --gpu-launcher, --browser-subprocess-path' combined with '--no-zygote'. Co-occurrence of --no-zygote with any of those four launcher overrides on a Chromium process image is the minimal sufficient condition for the exploit to land — the advisory states '--no-zygote, causing Chromium to fork/exec an attacker-controlled command'. Outside Chromium development this tuple is essentially never benign.
ATT&CKT1203 T1059 T1611

  • Internal red-team replaying the public PoC against patched 0.9.0 to validate the fix
  • Chromium fuzzing harnesses (ClusterFuzz, libFuzzer wrappers) that legitimately tweak subprocess launchers
  • Pentest training labs intentionally hosting the vulnerable image
  • Crawl4AI maintainer self-testing in a sandboxed lab container

Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the InitiatingProcessParent chain. Confirm the parent is Crawl4AI's Python entrypoint (uvicorn / gunicorn / python -m crawl4ai). Capture the command that follows the launcher-prefix flag — that string is the attacker's RCE payload. CONTAIN — Kill the parent Crawl4AI service, isolate the container/host from the network, snapshot the container filesystem and memory for forensics. Patch the image to crawl4ai >= 0.9.0 and set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN. 3. HUNT — Walk DeviceProcessEvents children of the Chromium PID for shells (bash, sh, busybox, cmd.exe), staging tools (curl, wget, nc, ncat, base64, python -c), and credential-access (cat /proc/self/environ, /var/run/secrets/**, AWS meta

Chromium subprocess override spawns non-Chromium child (Crawl4AI RCE post-exploitation) AIInstallation High
Process-tree detection for the moment the Crawl4AI exploit lands: a Chromium parent invoked with --browser-subprocess-path / --renderer-cmd-prefix / --utility-cmd-prefix / --gpu-launcher fork/execs a child that is NOT another Chromium binary. The launcher-prefix switches are specifically designed to replace the child-process launch command, so any non-Chromium child of such a parent is the attacker's payload running as the container runtime user. Rationale: The advisory says the launcher-prefix flags 'replace a child-process launch command...causing Chromium to fork/exec an attacker-controlled command as the container's runtime user'. The detection encodes that directly: parent is Chromium, parent cmdline contains one of the four advisory-named switches, child is not another Chromium helper. This is the on-disk fingerprint of the RCE actually executing.
ATT&CKT1203 T1059 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chromium browser developers' build/regression harnesses (these flags are documented Chromium dev features)
  • Headless Chromium fuzzing infrastructure (ClusterFuzz / libFuzzer wrappers)
  • Internal red-team replay of the PoC against patched 0.9.0 instances
  • Chromium release pipelines running automated subprocess tests
  • Researchers detonating the public PoC in isolated honeypot containers
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("chromium-build", "chrome-buildbot", "clusterfuzz")) and not (FileName in~ ("clusterfuzz", "libfuzzer", "asan_symbolize"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE — Capture the child ProcessCommandLine — that is the attacker's RCE payload. Common shapes: /bin/sh -c '<curl|wget> <stager>', python -c, bash with base64, /usr/bin/id, /bin/cat /proc/self/environ. Identify the host: get container ID via DeviceName / aid and confirm it is running crawl4ai <= 0.8.9. 2. CONTAIN — Kill the Crawl4AI container, pull a forensic snapshot, isolate the node from network. Rotate ALL secrets reachable from the container runtime user (env, mounted secrets, cloud IMDS tokens, DB creds, OAuth tokens). Block the source IP at WAF. Patch image to crawl4ai >= 0.9.0 and set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN. 3. HUNT — From the child PID walk its descendants: shells, reverse-shell tools (nc, ncat, socat, python -c 'import socket'), staging downloads (curl/wget to non-Chromium-update destinations), credential access (cat /var/run/secrets/**, IMDS 169.254.169.254). Pivot DeviceNetworkEvents off the container for new outbound destinations in the 30 minutes after exploit time. Sea

Crawl4AI Python process writes to Linux persistence path (GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 exploitation) AIInstallation High
Detects the actual on-disk artifact of the Crawl4AI path-traversal RCE: a python process whose command line references crawl4ai writing to a cron drop-in, profile.d, an SSH authorized_keys, or a shell rc-file. These targets are explicitly named in the advisory as the RCE escalation paths from arbitrary file write. Rationale: Article explicitly enumerates the RCE escalation paths: 'overwriting a shell rc-file, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, a cron entry, or a Python module on the import path.' The path list, combined with python/uvicorn/gunicorn as the writing process (the runtime under which crawl4ai executes per the affected file crawl4ai/async_crawler_strategy.py), is high-fidelity because legitimate python web services do not write to these locations. The crawl4ai cmdline tag elevates severity but is not required for the alert. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-365w-hqf6-vxfg/ • https://dev.to/cverports/ghsa-vx9w-5cx4-9796-crawl4ai-when-web-scrapers-become-file-servers-3kh0
ATT&CKT1505 T1098.004 T1053.003 T1546.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible / Chef / Puppet runs that shell out via a python wrapper to deploy cron drop-ins to /etc/cron.d/
  • cloud-init or container entrypoint scripts populating /etc/profile.d/ on first boot
  • SaltStack pip-installed states writing authorized_keys via python user.present
  • Pip-installed config-management tools deploying shell rc-files for service users
  • Developer running crawl4ai locally with a quirky configured downloads_path that happens to overlap a profile location
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/usr/lib/ansible","/usr/lib/salt","/opt/puppetlabs","/var/lib/cloud/") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","salt-call","puppet","cloud-init"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DeviceFileEvents / ImFileEvent for the host within 1h either side of the hit; read the written file's contents (is it an attacker shell key, a cron line invoking curl|bash, a tampered rc-file?); run `pip show crawl4ai` on the host to confirm vulnerable version <=0.8.9 and check whether the Docker /crawl endpoint is reachable without CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN. 2) Contain: stop the crawl4ai service/container, revert the written file from backup, rotate any SSH keys present in authorized_keys, remove unknown cron entries, and immediately upgrade to 0.9.0 OR set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN as the temporary workaround. 3) Hunt: pivot on UC2 inventory to find every other host running crawl4ai <=0.8.9, replay UC3 to find any spawned shells/reverse-connects, and review web/proxy logs for inbound POSTs to /crawl from external IPs that immediately preceded the write.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/cron.weekly/","/etc/cron.monthly/","/etc/profile.d/"))
    or (FolderPath has "/.ssh/" and FileName =~ "authorized_keys")
    or (FileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_login") and FolderPath !startswith "/etc/skel")
| extend Crawl4AIContext = iff(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","async_crawler_strategy","docker_server:app"), "crawl4ai", "other-python")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, Crawl4AIContext
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/cron.d/","/etc/cron.daily/","/etc/cron.hourly/","/etc/cron.weekly/","/etc/cron.monthly/","/etc/profile.d/"))
    or (TargetFilePath has "/.ssh/" and TargetFileName =~ "authorized_keys")
    or (TargetFileName in~ (".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile",".zshrc",".bash_login") and TargetFilePath !startswith "/etc/skel")
| extend Crawl4AIContext = iff(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","async_crawler_strategy","docker_server:app"), "crawl4ai", "other-python")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, Crawl4AIContext
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Crawl4AI package inventory (<= 0.8.9, pre-patch for GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory hunt for hosts running pip:crawl4ai at or below 0.8.9, the affected range called out in the advisory. Output the device list so the SOC can prioritise patching to 0.9.0 or applying the CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN workaround before the file-write detection (UC1) catches actual exploitation. Rationale: Advisory pins the affected range as pip:crawl4ai <= 0.8.9 with the fix in 0.9.0. Inventory hunt narrowed by package_manager=pip + name=crawl4ai is exact — no false matches against unrelated software. Joining DeviceInfo to flag internet-facing hosts surfaces the highest-priority targets first since the Docker /crawl HTTP sink is reachable unauthenticated by default. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer workstations with crawl4ai installed in a venv for testing — usually low-value but still worth tracking
  • Already-patched hosts where DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory hasn't refreshed yet (DAR sync lag, typical 12-24h)
  • Forked/vendored copies of crawl4ai that pin to an old version intentionally but aren't reachable from the internet
  • CI build agents that pip-install crawl4ai per job and tear down — appear in inventory briefly
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate each affected device — confirm whether it's a server running the Docker image (high risk, default-unauth /crawl endpoint) vs a dev workstation using the SDK against attacker-controlled URLs (medium risk). 2) Contain: schedule emergency upgrade to >=0.9.0 for any internet-facing server; for hosts that can't immediately patch, set CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN and confine the downloads_path to a dedicated volume mounted nosuid/nodev as an unprivileged user. 3) Hunt: for each affected host, run UC1 over the last 30 days to surface any historical file-write exploitation that pre-dated this detection going live.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName =~ "crawl4ai"
| extend MajorVer = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend MinorVer = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| extend PatchVer = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where MajorVer == 0 and (MinorVer < 8 or (MinorVer == 8 and PatchVer <= 9))
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, PublicIP, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName =~ "crawl4ai"
| extend MajorVer = toint(extract(@"^(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion)), MinorVer = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion)), PatchVer = toint(extract(@"^\d+\.\d+\.(\d+)", 1, SoftwareVersion))
| where MajorVer == 0 and (MinorVer < 8 or (MinorVer == 8 and PatchVer <= 9))
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, OSPlatform, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, IsInternetFacing, PublicIP
| order by IsInternetFacing desc
#event_simpleName=InstalledApplication SoftwareName=/^crawl4ai$/i
| regex("^0\\.([0-7]\\.|8\\.[0-9]$|8\\.[0-9][^0-9])", field=SoftwareVersion)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion], function=count())
APPLICATION
| inputlookup software_inventory.csv where package_manager="pip" AND package_name="crawl4ai" | rex field=package_version "^(?<major>\d+)\.(?<minor>\d+)\.(?<patch>\d+)" | where major=0 AND (minor<8 OR (minor=8 AND patch<=9)) | table host package_name package_version last_seen | sort - last_seen
Python crawl4ai process spawns shell or persistence helper (post-exploitation child) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the post-exploitation pivot from the Crawl4AI arbitrary file write: the python/uvicorn worker that exposed the vulnerable HTTP / Playwright crawler spawning a shell, crontab, ssh-keygen, or curl/wget. The vulnerable runtime should not normally fork these binaries. Rationale: Advisory names crawl4ai/async_crawler_strategy.py as the vulnerable file and the unauthenticated Docker /crawl endpoint (which runs the FastAPI app via uvicorn) as the reachable sink. A normal Crawl4AI worker does not exec shells, crontab, ssh-keygen, or curl — those are the obvious next steps after writing an attacker-controlled file (chmod the dropped payload, trigger the cron, fetch a second stage). Constrained to the parent-cmdline crawl4ai marker so it does not fire on generic python child-process noise. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 • https://dev.to/cverports/ghsa-5882-5rx9-xgxp-crawl4ai-rce-hook-line-and-sinker-into-your-docker-container-3l1l
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately invoking Playwright's bundled headless-chromium launcher which forks shell-like helpers on some distros
  • Container entrypoint scripts using sh -c to wrap the python crawl4ai server startup — would appear as parent=python child=sh once at boot
  • Developer using crawl4ai notebook / REPL that shells out via os.system or subprocess.run for debugging
  • Crawl4AI extension hooks (custom on_page hooks) that legitimately call curl/wget — should be reviewed and allow-listed by parent cmdline of the specific hook script
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/playwright/driver","playwright install","chromium --type=")) and not (FileName == "sh" and ProcessCommandLine has "-c" and ProcessCommandLine has "uvicorn")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full process tree (DeviceProcessEvents | extend ProcessGroup = … or `pstree` on host); read the child command line for indicators of fetch-and-exec (curl|bash, wget -O -, chmod +x then ./payload); correlate to UC1 hits on the same host within 5min either side. 2) Contain: kill the crawl4ai worker, isolate the host from network, snapshot memory + disk, rotate any credentials accessible from that container (env vars, mounted secrets, IMDS). 3) Hunt: pivot on outbound NetworkConnectIP4 from the python process during the same window to identify attacker C2; review web logs for the upstream POST /crawl that triggered exploitation and the attacker URL that returned the malicious Content-Disposition.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "python" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","async_crawler_strategy","docker_server:app")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","ksh","crontab","ssh-keygen","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","async_crawler_strategy","docker_server:app")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/bash","/sh","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/crontab","/ssh-keygen","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP request with spoofed 'auth-user: service-brother' header (@acastellon/auth GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests carrying the literal 'auth-user: service-brother' header — the exact marker that short-circuits validateToken() in @acastellon/auth <2.3.0 before legacy/JWT/OIDC validation runs. Any external/unauthenticated request matching this signature is exploitation of the bypass. Rationale: Targets the article's exact bypass marker — the literal 'auth-user: service-brother' header value that the GHSA names as the validateToken() short-circuit trigger. Detection must run at WAF/proxy/app layer because Defender XDR endpoint tables do not capture custom HTTP request headers (noted in defender_kql comment). The Sentinel union covers four realistic landing places: CommonSecurityLog (third-party WAFs), AzureDiagnostics (App Gateway / Front Door WAF / App Service), ImWebSession (ASIM normalised), and W3CIISLog (IIS in front of Node). No external sources cross-checked — niche npm GHSA with no CVE, no campaign attribution, and no second-source coverage expected.
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal service-to-service calls from the real service-brother microservice originating from RFC1918 / known service CIDR
  • Application security testing tools (Burp, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei) replaying the public PoC against pre-prod environments
  • Internal red-team or purple-team exercises verifying the v2.3.0 patch landed
  • Vendor pentest engagements including this advisory in their test plan
  • SOC itself replaying the marker through WAF to validate a new block rule
Suppression filter
| where ExternalSrc == "yes"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull source IP, destination hostname, full URL. Run `npm ls @acastellon/auth` on the destination host — if version >= 2.3.0 the bypass is patched and this is likely scanner noise. Check the ExternalSrc enrichment column: internal source + known service-brother CIDR = closeable. 2) Contain: External source + destination version < 2.3.0 = confirmed exploitation. Block source IP at WAF/edge, rotate any session tokens or JWTs minted by the application in the suspect time window, force re-auth on the affected app, and capture full request bodies for IR. 3) Hunt: Pivot on source IP for 24h of activity across all applications. Search for follow-up requests carrying 'is-admin: true' or other 'is-*' privilege-claim headers from the same IP (see UC3). Review downstream services that trust the auth-user header for anomalous service-brother activity (DB writes, admin actions, token mints).
// @acastellon/auth ships as a Node.js dependency — HTTP request headers are NOT in Defender XDR endpoint tables. This query surfaces internet-facing Node.js listeners on hosts likely to be running the vulnerable middleware; the actual header inspection must run on WAF/proxy logs (see sentinel_kql / datadog_query).
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","nodejs.exe","pm2.exe")
| where LocalPort in (80,443,3000,4000,5000,8080,8443)

| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" or ActionType == "ConnectionAccepted"
| summarize InboundConns=count(), DistinctRemoteIPs=dcount(RemoteIP), arg_max(Timestamp, RemoteIP, RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, LocalPort
| where InboundConns > 0
| extend Advisory="GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw — verify @acastellon/auth dependency on this host"
| order by InboundConns desc

Vulnerable @acastellon/auth (<2.3.0) package on disk + internet-facing Node.js listener AIWeaponization High
Hunts hosts where the @acastellon/auth dependency tree is present on disk (node_modules/@acastellon/auth/package.json or auth.js) and joins against internet-facing Node.js listener telemetry to prioritise the most exposed targets. This is the actual attack surface for GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw and feeds the patching workstream. Rationale: Targets the article's specifically-named affected package '@acastellon/auth v2.2.0' by hunting the npm install footprint on disk (node_modules/@acastellon/auth/package.json and auth.js). The Defender query cross-joins with internet-facing Node.js listener telemetry to prioritise the most-exposed hosts for emergency patching. Path matching uses contains+all rather than literal escaped paths because npm's @-scoped package directory naming is consistent enough (and avoids fragile JSON/regex backslash escaping). No external corroboration searched — GHSA is the only authoritative source for this niche package.
ATT&CKT1190 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dev / sandbox / lab hosts intentionally kept at v2.2.0 for regression testing of the v2.3.0 fix
  • Backup or archived application snapshots being restored on a non-production host
  • Security researcher / red-team / purple-team host reproducing the advisory PoC
  • Container image build caches that retain old node_modules layers despite the running container shipping v2.3.0
  • Internal package mirror or artifact registry that holds all historical versions for auditing
Suppression filter
| where DvcHostname !contains "-dev" and DvcHostname !contains "-sandbox" and DvcHostname !contains "-lab" and DvcHostname !contains "-qa"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Read package.json on the affected device — `Get-Content '<path>\node_modules\@acastellon\auth\package.json' | ConvertFrom-Json | Select version` (or `jq .version` on Linux). If version >= 2.3.0 close as patched. 2) Contain: version < 2.3.0 AND InternetFacing == 'yes' → page the app owner, fast-track the bump to 2.3.0+, AND in the meantime front the app with a WAF rule blocking inbound requests carrying 'auth-user: service-brother' (mitigates exposure while patching). 3) Hunt: For every vulnerable+internet-facing host, run UC1 across the prior 90 days against the destination FQDN. Any hits = treat as candidate compromise, escalate to IR, and review downstream services that trust the auth-user/is-* headers for anomalous service-brother activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath contains "node_modules" and FolderPath contains "acastellon" and FolderPath contains "auth"
| where FileName in~ ("package.json","auth.js")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), arg_max(Timestamp, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName) by DeviceName, FileName
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","nodejs.exe")
    | where LocalPort in (80,443,3000,4000,5000,8080,8443)
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | summarize NodeInboundConns=count() by DeviceName
) on DeviceName
| extend InternetFacing = iif(isnotempty(NodeInboundConns) and NodeInboundConns > 0, "yes", "unknown"), Advisory="GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw — @acastellon/auth < 2.3.0"
| project DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FirstSeen, LastSeen, NodeInboundConns, InternetFacing, Advisory
| order by InternetFacing desc, LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath contains "node_modules" and TargetFilePath contains "acastellon" and TargetFilePath contains "auth"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("package.json","auth.js")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), arg_max(TimeGenerated, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName) by DvcHostname, TargetFileName
| extend Advisory="GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw — @acastellon/auth < 2.3.0 (check package.json version field)"
| order by LastSeen desc

Spoofable privilege-claim headers (is-admin / is-*) downstream of @acastellon/auth bypass AIExploitation Medium
Detects HTTP requests carrying 'is-admin: true' or other 'is-*' privilege-asserting headers. The article's v2.3.0 fix explicitly adds sanitisation for incoming 'is-*' headers because the vulnerable middleware passed them through to downstream services that trusted them, enabling privilege escalation once validateToken() was bypassed. Co-occurrence with 'service-brother' makes this the highest-confidence post-bypass primitive. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit fix note: 'Always sanitize incoming auth-user and is-* headers' — meaning the v2.3.0 patch identifies 'is-*' headers as a privilege-escalation primitive when paired with downstream services that trust them. The 'is-admin: true' header appears verbatim in the article's example request. PairedWithBypass enrichment promotes the highest-confidence hit (is-* co-occurring with service-brother in the same request). The Sentinel query filters out internal traffic without bypass co-occurrence to keep FP rate down. No external corroboration searched — niche GHSA with no CVE / campaign mapping.
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal frontend → backend service-mesh traffic where some apps legitimately propagate 'is-' prefixed feature-flag headers (e.g. 'is-feature-x: true')
  • Health-check / synthetic monitoring tooling that exercises admin endpoints with explicit privilege flags
  • QA test harnesses that set 'is-admin: true' against staging to bypass paywall / role checks
  • Pentest / bug-bounty researcher demonstrating the advisory PoC
  • WAF rule auditing where the SOC itself replays the marker headers to validate the new block rule
Suppression filter
| where PairedWithBypass == "yes" or ExternalSrc == "yes"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Check if source IP is internal (service-mesh) or external. Pull the destination URL — admin / internal API paths are highest-risk. If the same source IP also fired UC1 (auth-user: service-brother) within ±5 minutes, OR PairedWithBypass == 'yes' on this event, escalate immediately as confirmed exploitation chain. 2) Contain: External source + admin-path destination → block source IP at WAF, invalidate any sessions / API tokens / role grants minted on the destination service since the first hit, force re-auth. Notify the application owner that downstream services trusting 'is-*' headers must either be hardened or fronted by a header-stripping proxy. 3) Hunt: Across the prior 7 days, search for 'is-*: true' headers from the same source IP against any application. Review downstream service logs on the destination host (DB writes, role assignments, token mints, admin UI actions) for activity consistent with an elevated principal that the actual auth-user wouldn't have authorised.
let privHeaders = dynamic(["is-admin","is-superuser","is-staff","is-root","is-internal","is-service"]);
let truthy = dynamic(["true","1","yes"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
        | where Message has_any (privHeaders) and Message has_any (truthy)
        | extend PairedWithBypass=iif(Message has "service-brother","yes","no")
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceTable="CommonSecurityLog", SrcIP=SourceIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, URL=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod, PairedWithBypass, Raw=Message),
    (AzureDiagnostics
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
        | where Category in ("ApplicationGatewayFirewallLog","FrontdoorWebApplicationFirewallLog","AppServiceHTTPLogs","FrontdoorAccessLog")
        | extend PropsStr=tostring(Properties)
        | where PropsStr has_any (privHeaders)
        | extend PairedWithBypass=iif(PropsStr has "service-brother","yes","no")
        | project TimeGenerated, SourceTable=Category, SrcIP=tostring(Properties.clientIP), DstHost=tostring(Properties.host), URL=tostring(Properties.requestUri), Method=tostring(Properties.httpMethod), PairedWithBypass, Raw=PropsStr)
)
| extend ExternalSrc=iif(SrcIP startswith "10." or SrcIP startswith "172.16." or SrcIP startswith "172.17." or SrcIP startswith "172.18." or SrcIP startswith "172.19." or SrcIP startswith "172.20." or SrcIP startswith "172.21." or SrcIP startswith "172.22." or SrcIP startswith "172.23." or SrcIP startswith "172.24." or SrcIP startswith "172.25." or SrcIP startswith "172.26." or SrcIP startswith "172.27." or SrcIP startswith "172.28." or SrcIP startswith "172.29." or SrcIP startswith "172.30." or SrcIP startswith "172.31." or SrcIP startswith "192.168.","no","yes"), Advisory="GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw — privilege-claim header on the wire"
| where PairedWithBypass == "yes" or ExternalSrc == "yes"
| order by PairedWithBypass desc, TimeGenerated desc

NetLicensing /token endpoint accessed from MCP server / Python process AIExploitation High
Hunts wire-level evidence of the netlicensing-mcp path-traversal exploit by flagging outbound HTTPS requests resolving to the NetLicensing /core/v2/rest/token endpoint that originate from a Python/MCP process. Under normal operation the MCP tools authenticate via header and rarely hit /token directly, so an unexpected hit on that path from the MCP host is the post-normalization fingerprint of `netlicensing_get_product('../token')`. Rationale: Uses the exact `/core/v2/rest/token` URL path the article names as the post-normalization sink (`client.py:143`, `server.py:336`). The MCP server's legitimate auth path is the API-key HTTP header — it does NOT normally GET /token — so any /token hit from the MCP host process is high-fidelity for either successful exploitation or attempted probing of the bypass. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1212 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate netlicensing_get_token / netlicensing_list_tokens tool invocations (these DO call /token by design and will look identical at the wire)
  • NetLicensing admin / portal browser sessions opening the token-management page from a developer workstation
  • Initial MCP server bootstrap that resolves the token to verify credentials
  • CI/CD smoke tests that exercise the token endpoint against a staging NetLicensing tenant
  • Internal scripts using httpx that legitimately enumerate /token for service inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("netlicensing_get_token","netlicensing_list_tokens","--init","--healthcheck"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess tree on the host; confirm the Python process was launched as netlicensing-mcp (look for `netlicensing_mcp.server` or `mcp[cli]` in the parent command line) and check the same process's prior /product/ requests in DeviceNetworkEvents (last 10 min). If the parent MCP client called a tool other than `netlicensing_get_token`/`netlicensing_list_tokens`, treat as exploitation. Step 2 — Contain: rotate ALL NetLicensing APIKEY tokens visible to that tenant via the NetLicensing console, prioritising any with `ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN`; revoke the API key the MCP server itself was running with. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the API key value (if leaked) across egress proxy logs for the next 24h for use from any other IP; sweep all hosts running netlicensing-mcp 0.1.5 / commit c8a3fec and pin to a patched version including the `_validated_path` segment validator.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/core/v2/rest/token"
   or (RemoteUrl has_any ("netlicensing.io","netlicensing.labs64.com","go.netlicensing.io") and RemoteUrl endswith "/token")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","python","pwsh.exe","node.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("netlicensing_mcp","netlicensing-mcp","mcp[cli]","netlicensing_get_product")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,

Path traversal characters in netlicensing_get_product MCP tool invocation AIWeaponization High
Detects an MCP client passing a path-traversal payload as the `product_number` argument to `netlicensing_get_product`, captured in the host process command line or the MCP server application log. This is the application-layer fingerprint of GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 — the literal string that flows through `tools/products.py:22` before httpx normalization erases it. Rationale: Pivots on the literal traversal payloads the article remediation suggests adding regression tests for — `../token`, `%2e%2e`, `%2f`, `%5c` — combined with the article-named MCP tool symbol `netlicensing_get_product` and package `netlicensing_mcp`. These strings only co-occur in legitimate use if a developer is testing exploit detection. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1190 T1212
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the GHSA PoC on a developer workstation
  • Regression tests asserting the `_validated_path` fix rejects the listed payloads (the test names themselves contain `../token`)
  • Detection-engineering team building Sigma/KQL coverage and pasting the payload into a shell to test
  • Static analysis / SAST scanner output piped to a console that includes the vulnerable code snippet
  • An MCP client built by an internal team that legitimately encodes slashes in product numbers (unlikely — NetLicensing product numbers are alphanumeric)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","unittest","regression","test_traversal","_test.py") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","test_traversal"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the parent of the python process (IDE / shell / remote agent) and the user; confirm whether the host is a known developer workstation with the GHSA repo cloned. Pull the MCP server's stdout/stderr (if logged) for the exact tool-call payload and whether the response contained a `number` field with an APIKEY value. Step 2 — Contain: if the MCP server's logs show a successful response to `../token`, immediately rotate the NetLicensing API key the server runs as and any APIKEY tokens listed in the response; if production, isolate the host. Step 3 — Hunt: across the fleet, list every host with netlicensing-mcp installed (`pip show netlicensing-mcp` or DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory) and pin to the patched release; sweep last 30 days of DeviceProcessEvents for the same payload strings against any user, not just the triggering one.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("netlicensing_mcp","netlicensing-mcp","netlicensing_get_product")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "netlicensing_get_product"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "product_number"
   or ProcessCommandLine has "/product/"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (
        "../token", "..\\token",
        "%2e%2e/", "%2e%2e%2f", "%2e%2e%5c",
        "%2ftoken", "%5ctoken",
        "..%2f", "..%5c",
        "/product/../", "\\product\\..\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (SecurityEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where EventID == 4688
   | where NewProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe")

   | extend Cmd = SyslogMessage)
| where Cmd has_any ("netlicensing_get_product","netlicensing_mcp","product_number")

URL-encoded path traversal targeting NetLicensing /product/ REST API AIExploitation Medium
Hunts URL-encoded path traversal variants (`%2e%2e`, `%2f`, `%5c`, double-encoded `%252e`) appearing inside the path segment of a request to a NetLicensing REST API. The GHSA explicitly calls these out as remediation regression-test inputs and they bypass naive `..` string filters at WAF / proxy layers but normalize identically in `httpx` to redirect the call to `/token`. Rationale: Uses the exact four encoded payloads the article lists as remediation regression tests — `%2e%2e`, `%2f`, `%5c`, and the implicit `..` — scoped to the `/product/` path and NetLicensing host to keep noise low. Double-encoded `%252e` is added because WAFs typically decode once and pass the rest through to httpx where the second decode triggers the traversal. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1190 T1027 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Product numbers that legitimately contain percent-encoded characters (rare — NetLicensing product numbers are typically slug-style)
  • Security scanners (Burp / ZAP / Nuclei) running an authorized assessment against the MCP host
  • SOAR-driven detection rule validation that replays the encoded payloads as part of purple-team exercises
  • WAF in inline mode that already rewrote / blocked the request but still logged the original URL
  • Browser-based admin tools to NetLicensing UI that include encoded query parameters (these hit /ui/ not /product/ so should not match)
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Nuclei","Burp","OWASP ZAP","sqlmap") and SourceIP in ("<sec-team-scanner-cidrs>"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: extract the source IP / user / host of the request and decode the URL fully (two passes for `%252e`) to confirm it resolves to `/token`, `/auth`, or another sensitive endpoint after `..` collapse. Pull the matching response status code and body size from the proxy log — a 200 with non-trivial body suggests a successful read. Step 2 — Contain: if the response was successful, treat any APIKEY/SHOP credentials in the response body as compromised; rotate the API key the calling MCP server runs with via the NetLicensing console. Step 3 — Hunt: search the prior 24h of proxy logs for the same source IP issuing other unusual `/product/` paths or any `/token`, `/license`, `/payment` endpoint hits; pivot on the user-agent string across the wider fleet for related probing.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("netlicensing.io","netlicensing.labs64.com","go.netlicensing.io")
| where RemoteUrl has "/product/"
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)/product/[^?#]*(%2e%2e|%252e%252e|%2ftoken|%5ctoken|\.\.%2f|\.\.%5c|\.\.%252f)"

          RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct

Behavioral: NetLicensing /product/ traversal followed by /token endpoint hit within 5 minutes AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a NetLicensing `/product/` request carrying a traversal pattern with a follow-up `/token` endpoint hit from the same source within 5 minutes, capturing the exploit-then-probe behavioural sequence an attacker uses to confirm the GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8 bypass succeeded. Either signal alone is medium-fidelity; the pair within a short window is high-fidelity. Rationale: Implements the reviewer-suggested behavioural sequence: traversal on `/product/` and `/token` hit from the same source within 5 minutes (`WindowSec = 300`). Uses the exact URL paths the article identifies (`/product/{product_number}` source and `/core/v2/rest/token` sink) so the join is anchored on article-specific strings, not generic traversal-then-anything patterns. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hxpf-9xvq-wph8
ATT&CKT1212 T1087
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the GHSA PoC end-to-end (would generate both events)
  • Red team / purple team exercise scripted to confirm the bypass against staging
  • Penetration test against a NetLicensing-using application within an authorized engagement
  • WAF in passive/log-only mode allowing the traversal through, with downstream Token API still legitimately invoked by another tenant request from the same egress IP
  • Shared NAT egress IP where one tenant's product traversal and another tenant's legitimate /token call coincidentally land within 5 min
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull both raw requests; confirm the traversal path on `/product/` decodes to `..` and that the `/token` response was 200 with body size >200 bytes (the redacted API key response is ~150 bytes; the unredacted one is larger). Identify the calling MCP client / user via auth headers or sessionContext. Step 2 — Contain: rotate the API key the MCP server runs with via the NetLicensing console; if the unredacted /token response was 200, treat every APIKEY token in the affected NetLicensing account as compromised and rotate them, prioritising `ROLE_APIKEY_ADMIN`. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the source IP across the prior 30 days for any other `/product/` requests with non-ASCII identifiers or other anomalous segments (`/license/../`, `/payment/../`); upgrade all netlicensing-mcp instances to a release that includes the `_validated_path` segment validator.
let WindowSec = 300;
let Traversal = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("netlicensing.io","netlicensing.labs64.com","go.netlicensing.io")
    | where RemoteUrl has "/product/"
    | where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)/product/[^?#]*(\.\.|%2e%2e|%2ftoken|%5ctoken|\.\.%2f|\.\.%5c)"
    | project ProductTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ProductUrl = RemoteUrl,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let TokenHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any ("netlicensing.io","netlicensing.labs64.com","go.netlicensing.io")
    | where RemoteUrl has "/core/v2/rest/token"
    | project TokenTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, TokenUrl = RemoteUrl;
Traversal
| join kind=inner TokenHits on DeviceId
| where TokenTime between (ProductTime .. ProductTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TokenTime, ProductTime)
| project ProductTime, TokenTime, DelaySec, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProductUrl, TokenUrl
| order by ProductTime desc
let WindowSec = 300;
let Traversal = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has_any ("netlicensing.io","netlicensing.labs64.com","go.netlicensing.io")
    | where RequestURL has "/product/"

    | project ProductTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, ProductUrl = RequestURL, RequestClientApplication;
let TokenHits = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has_any ("netlicensing.io","netlicensing.labs64.com","go.netlicensing.io")
    | where RequestURL has "/core/v2/rest/token"
    | project TokenTime = TimeGenerated, SourceIP, TokenUrl = RequestURL;
Traversal
| join kind=inner TokenHits on SourceIP
| where TokenTime between (ProductTime .. ProductTime + WindowSec * 1s)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TokenTime, ProductTime)
| project ProductTime, TokenTime, DelaySec, SourceIP, SourceUserName,
          RequestClientApplication, ProductUrl, TokenUrl
| order by ProductTime desc
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=443
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/netlicensing(\.io|\.labs64\.com)$/i}, field=[aid, ContextProcessId], include=[DomainName])

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
| count > 0

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Script interpreter spawned by explorer.exe from removable-drive LNK target
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — USB worm spreads crypto-stealing malware via Windows shortcut files
Installation. Script interpreter spawned by explorer.exe from removable-drive LNK target AIDelivery Medium
Detects wscript/cscript/cmd/powershell/mshta launched by Explorer with a .lnk reference in the command line — the documented worm entry where a user double-clicks the malicious shortcut on a USB stick. Article-specific because Microsoft calls out wscript.exe/cscript.exe as the post-LNK execution surface. Rationale: Article: 'the infection process starts with the victim opening the LNK file' and recommends monitoring 'process activity on wscript.exe and cscript.exe' with 'unusual child processes'. Parent explorer.exe + script interpreter + .lnk in cmdline is the article's documented entry shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/security/blog/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin double-clicking a legitimate .lnk shortcut that targets cmd.exe (e.g. ‘Open admin shell’)
  • Software installers shipping a .lnk that invokes wscript for first-run setup
  • IT-deployed Start-menu shortcuts that wrap a PowerShell script
  • Developer .lnk shortcuts to dev-shell environments
  • Legitimate USB autorun launchers from vendor toolkits
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Microsoft.Update","OneDrive","VSCode"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the .lnk file's FolderPath — if it lives on a removable drive (D:/E:/F:) with FileOriginUrl null, treat as worm. Pull the LNK target (InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and look up the dropped script body. 2) Contain: isolate the device, block the script SHA256, eject the removable drive, and enumerate other endpoints that mounted the same USB volume via DeviceEvents UsbDriveMounted. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for new .lnk creations on Documents/Downloads/Desktop with same FileName as a recently hidden document, and DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound localhost:9050 (Tor SOCKS) connections from script-interpreter parents.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".lnk"
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("Program Files","Windows\\System32"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","mshta.exe")
| where CommandLine has ".lnk"
| where not(Account endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Script Interpreter Spawned by Explorer With LNK In Command Line
id: 7c4b6e92-3a1e-4d77-9c4a-4b8a1b9d2f01
description: Detects script interpreter spawned by Explorer with a .lnk reference in the command line, consistent with the USB LNK worm initial-access step described by Microsoft.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/usb-worm-spreads-crypto-stealing-malware-via-windows-shortcut-files/
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\explorer.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '.lnk'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\explorer.exe OR *\\Explorer.EXE) @Image:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe) @CommandLine:*.lnk*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/explorer\.exe$/i | ImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript|cmd|powershell|pwsh|mshta)\.exe$/i | regex("\.lnk", field=CommandLine)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe") Processes.process="*.lnk*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user,"\\$$")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="explorer.exe" Processes.process_name IN ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe") Processes.process="*.lnk*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where NOT match(user,"\\$$")
Scheduled task created with USB / volume-arrival trigger (worm persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects schtasks.exe or PowerShell Register-ScheduledTask invocations whose trigger XML/parameters reference USB / removable-media / volume-arrival event sources — the worm's documented mechanism for noticing newly inserted USB drives and re-infecting them. Rationale: Article: 'The worm creates a scheduled task that monitors for newly connected USB storage devices.' On Windows, USB-arrival event triggers come from those exact ETW providers (Kernel-PnP, DriverFrameworks-UserMode) or are configured via /sc onevent and Register-ScheduledTask -Trigger; collocating them with task-creation tools is a high-signal pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1091/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1091
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR / DLP agents installing legitimate USB-monitoring tasks (CrowdStrike, Sophos, Ivanti)
  • SCCM / Intune endpoint management package that registers a removable-media task
  • Manual IT troubleshooting using /sc onevent to chase a driver issue
  • Backup software registering volume-arrival tasks for external-drive backups
  • Vendor toolkit installers (e.g. printer drivers) registering a Kernel-PnP task
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Microsoft Corporation","CrowdStrike","Sophos","Ivanti","VMware"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task XML (schtasks /Query /TN <name> /XML) and review the Actions block — confirm the Exec path is on a removable drive or user-writable path. Check task author and signer. 2) Contain: schtasks /Delete /TN <name>, kill the registering parent process, and isolate the device. 3) Hunt: across the fleet, search DeviceRegistryEvents for new keys under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Schedule\TaskCache\Tasks created in the last 30 days whose Path action targets %APPDATA%/%TEMP%/removable letters.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("schtasks","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTaskTrigger")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP","DriverFrameworks-UserMode","DeviceArrival","VolumeChange","Removable","WPD-MTPClassDriver","USB","onevent")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","TiWorker.exe","setup.exe"))
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("schtasks","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTaskTrigger")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP","DriverFrameworks-UserMode","DeviceArrival","VolumeChange","Removable","WPD-MTPClassDriver","USB","onevent")
| where not(Account endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Created With USB or Volume Arrival Trigger
id: 4d9c2af1-7b3c-4f5a-9c1d-3e2b6a5c8d44
description: Detects creation of a scheduled task whose trigger references USB / removable-media / volume-arrival event sources, consistent with the LNK USB worm's persistence mechanism for re-infecting newly inserted drives.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/usb-worm-spreads-crypto-stealing-malware-via-windows-shortcut-files/
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1091
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  selection_create:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'schtasks'
      - 'Register-ScheduledTask'
      - 'New-ScheduledTaskTrigger'
  selection_usb:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP'
      - 'DriverFrameworks-UserMode'
      - 'DeviceArrival'
      - 'VolumeChange'
      - 'Removable'
      - 'WPD-MTPClassDriver'

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*schtasks* OR *Register-ScheduledTask* OR *New-ScheduledTaskTrigger*) @CommandLine:(*Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP* OR *DriverFrameworks-UserMode* OR *DeviceArrival* OR *VolumeChange* OR *Removable* OR *WPD-MTPClassDriver* OR *onevent*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(schtasks|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i | regex("(?i)(schtasks|Register-ScheduledTask|New-ScheduledTaskTrigger)", field=CommandLine) | regex("(?i)(Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP|DriverFrameworks-UserMode|DeviceArrival|VolumeChange|Removable|WPD-MTPClassDriver|onevent)", field=CommandLine)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*schtasks*" OR Processes.process="*Register-ScheduledTask*" OR Processes.process="*New-ScheduledTaskTrigger*") (Processes.process="*Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP*" OR Processes.process="*DriverFrameworks-UserMode*" OR Processes.process="*DeviceArrival*" OR Processes.process="*VolumeChange*" OR Processes.process="*Removable*" OR Processes.process="*WPD-MTPClassDriver*" OR Processes.process="*onevent*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") (Processes.process="*schtasks*" OR Processes.process="*Register-ScheduledTask*" OR Processes.process="*New-ScheduledTaskTrigger*") (Processes.process="*Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP*" OR Processes.process="*DriverFrameworks-UserMode*" OR Processes.process="*DeviceArrival*" OR Processes.process="*VolumeChange*" OR Processes.process="*Removable*" OR Processes.process="*WPD-MTPClassDriver*" OR Processes.process="*onevent*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
attrib +h followed by .lnk creation impersonating hidden document (worm replacement) AIInstallation High
Detects the worm's signature replacement pattern: attrib.exe +h applied to a document file, followed within minutes by a .lnk shortcut with the same basename created in the same user directory (Documents/Downloads/Desktop). Article explicitly describes this as the propagation/persistence trick. Rationale: Article: 'the malware hides the originals and replaces them with malicious shortcuts bearing the same names'. The temporal join of attrib +h on a document + .lnk creation in the same user folder within minutes is uniquely characteristic of this worm and difficult to reproduce with legitimate software. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1564/001/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Some PDF editors that hide a working copy of a document while writing a .lnk to a recent-files folder
  • User running attrib +h via scripted backup followed by a Recent Items .lnk update by Explorer
  • Sync agents (OneDrive/Dropbox/Box) hiding tombstone files and emitting .lnk placeholders
  • Office Document Recovery sweeping AutoRecover with hidden attribute, plus Office shortcut refresh
  • Legacy installer cleanup that hides old document templates and creates Start menu .lnk
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OneDrive.exe","GoogleDriveFS.exe","Dropbox.exe","explorer.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the .lnk TargetExe via parse_lnk on the FolderPath — if it points to wscript.exe with a script in %APPDATA%/Temp or off a removable drive, treat as confirmed. Verify the hidden 'original' file still exists at the same FolderPath. 2) Contain: isolate device, unhide originals (attrib -h -s), delete the malicious .lnk files, and remove the persistence scheduled task. 3) Hunt: across the fleet, run the same join over 30d to find other infected users; pivot on the InitiatingProcessSHA256 of attrib's parent (it'll often be the worm dropper itself).
let HideEvents = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where FileName =~ "attrib.exe"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "+h"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".doc",".docx",".xls",".xlsx",".pdf",".pptx",".txt",".rtf")
    | project HideTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, AccountName, HideCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".lnk"
| where FolderPath has_any ("Documents","Downloads","Desktop")
| join kind=inner HideEvents on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (HideTime .. HideTime + 5m)
| project HideTime, LnkCreatedTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, HideCmd, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by HideTime desc
let HideEvents = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith @"\attrib.exe"
    | where CommandLine has "+h"
    | where CommandLine has_any (".doc",".docx",".xls",".xlsx",".pdf",".pptx",".txt")
    | project HideTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, HideCmd = CommandLine;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".lnk"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("Documents","Downloads","Desktop")
| join kind=inner HideEvents on $left.DvcHostname == $right.Computer
| where TimeGenerated between (HideTime .. HideTime + 5m)
| project HideTime, LnkTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, Account, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, HideCmd
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\attrib.exe OR *\\ATTRIB.EXE) @CommandLine:*+h* @CommandLine:(*.doc* OR *.xls* OR *.pdf* OR *.pptx* OR *.txt*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\attrib\.exe$/i | regex("\+h", field=CommandLine) | regex("(?i)\.(docx?|xlsx?|pdf|pptx?|txt|rtf)", field=CommandLine) | join({#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.lnk$/i | regex("(?i)\\\\(Documents|Downloads|Desktop)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)}, field=aid)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstAttrib max(_time) as lastAttrib from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="attrib.exe" Processes.process="*+h*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=inner dest [ | tstats `summariesonly` count as lnkCount min(_time) as lnkFirstSeen from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" (Filesystem.file_path="*Documents*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Downloads*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Desktop*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` ] | eval delta=lnkFirstSeen-firstAttrib | where delta > -10 AND delta < 300
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstAttrib max(_time) as lastAttrib from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="attrib.exe" Processes.process="*+h*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | join type=inner dest [ | tstats summariesonly=false count as lnkCount min(_time) as lnkFirstSeen from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" (Filesystem.file_path="*Documents*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Downloads*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Desktop*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` ] | eval delta=lnkFirstSeen-firstAttrib | where delta > -10 AND delta < 300
Worm RCE: file named 'cfile' dropped and executed by wscript/cscript (C2 EVAL) AICommand & Control High
Detects the worm's documented C2 EVAL primitive: JavaScript content downloaded to a file named exactly 'cfile' that is then executed by wscript.exe or cscript.exe. The combination of the literal filename 'cfile' as a wscript argument is article-specific. Rationale: Article: 'the malware downloads JavaScript content into a file named cfile, and executes it on the infected machine.' The literal filename 'cfile' as a script-host argument is article-specific and exceptionally low-noise. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal dev tooling that ships a script literally named cfile.js
  • Build scripts using a file argument called 'cfile' in CI runners
  • Legacy logon scripts using temp filenames that happen to match
  • Test/QA harnesses exercising wscript with arbitrary placeholder names
  • User-named scripts (rare but possible) in Documents or scratch folders
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("AzureDevOps","Jenkins","GitLab-Runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: get the FolderPath of the cfile drop and the SHA256; check for the JavaScript body matching the worm's EVAL handler (clipboard polling regex, BIP39 wordlists, references to ugate.exe / localhost:9050). 2) Contain: kill the wscript/cscript process, delete cfile + its parent script, remove the scheduled task, and isolate. 3) Hunt: cross-reference with DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from wscript.exe/cscript.exe to localhost:9050 within the same hour, and pull URL logs for the .onion staging host that delivered the JS.
let CfileDrop = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
    | where FileName =~ "cfile" or FileName endswith "cfile"
    | project DropTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DropFolder = FolderPath, DropParent = InitiatingProcessFileName, DropCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "cfile"
| join kind=inner CfileDrop on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (DropTime .. DropTime + 10m)
| project DropTime, ExecTime = Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, DropFolder, DropParent
| order by ExecTime desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has "cfile"
| where not(Account endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Wscript or Cscript Executing File Named cfile

Tor SOCKS proxy connection to localhost:9050 from clipper/script host AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound TCP connections to 127.0.0.1:9050 (Tor SOCKS) from non-Tor-browser processes — specifically wscript/cscript/curl/cmd/powershell or the article-named ugate.exe binary. Article explicitly flags 'connections to localhost:9050 and Tor proxy activity' as red flags for this campaign. Rationale: Article: 'connections to localhost:9050 and Tor proxy activity are red flags associated with this campaign', and explicitly names ugate.exe as the Tor binary. 127.0.0.1:9050 from non-Tor-browser processes is a near-perfect IOC for the documented C2 path. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1090/003/ • https://2019.www.torproject.org/docs/tor-manual.html.en
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Penetration testers running torsocks-wrapped commands
  • Anonymity-focused users running Tor Browser bundle but invoking curl from PS
  • Developer testing of a Tor SOCKS client from a script
  • Internal red-team operations using ugate-like binaries (unlikely to share that exact name)
  • Tor relay/middleman experiments on endpoints
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("Tor Browser","tor-browser","OnionShare"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of the initiating process; if FileName matches 'ugate.exe' confirm it's not a renamed tor.exe (compare VersionInfoOriginalFileName) and check whether tor.exe-like service is registered. 2) Contain: kill the process, block 127.0.0.1:9050 egress is impossible — instead block the offending binary by SHA256 and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search DeviceFileEvents for ugate.exe writes across the fleet; pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 to find the worm dropper and replay the kill chain (LNK → wscript → cfile → ugate).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "127.0.0.1" and RemotePort == 9050
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","ugate.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "ugate.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
VMConnection
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationIp == "127.0.0.1" and DestinationPort == 9050
| where ProcessName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","ugate.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, DestinationIp, DestinationPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Tor SOCKS Proxy Connection from Script Host or ugate.exe
id: a1c3e9b2-4d57-4f1e-9a2b-7c8d3e4f5a01
description: Detects outbound TCP connection to 127.0.0.1:9050 (Tor SOCKS) from wscript/cscript/curl/cmd/powershell or the worm-specific ugate.exe binary used by the LNK USB clipper malware.
references:

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=127.0.0.1 RemotePort=9050 | ContextImageFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript|curl|cmd|powershell|pwsh|ugate)\.exe$/i
NETWORK
