curl.exe spawned by script host with Tor SOCKS proxy flag (screenshot exfil) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects curl.exe spawned by wscript/cscript/cmd/powershell with a --socks5 / --socks5-hostname argument pointing at localhost:9050, or a .onion URL — matching the article's documented screenshot exfiltration path (curl to C2 over Tor every ~10s). Rationale: Article: 'captures five screenshots of the victim's screen every ten seconds and sends them to the C2 using the curl tool' plus 'connections to localhost:9050 and Tor proxy activity'. curl + SOCKS5/.onion + script-host parent is the cleanest signature for the documented exfil channel. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1113/
ATT&CKT1567 T1113 T1090.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher running curl against onion sites for benign research
  • Pentester using curl with --socks5 for engagement
  • Web-scraping automation script that legitimately proxies via Tor
  • Vendor diagnostic tools that test Tor connectivity
  • Power user invoking curl from PowerShell for personal anonymity
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("Tor Browser","Postman","Insomnia"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the destination URL from ProcessCommandLine; resolve the .onion or check for the literal localhost:9050 SOCKS pattern. Confirm the parent is wscript/cscript or ugate.exe (worm pattern) vs a human shell. 2) Contain: kill curl + parent script, remove scheduled task, isolate. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceFileEvents for screenshot-like writes (.png/.jpg/.bmp in %TEMP% or %APPDATA%) within 30s of each curl invocation; check for matching POST-shaped uploads. Search the fleet for any process invoking curl with --socks5 to localhost:9050 in the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--socks5","socks5h://","127.0.0.1:9050",".onion")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","ugate.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("--socks5","socks5h://","127.0.0.1:9050",".onion")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","ugate.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Curl Tor SOCKS Proxy Or Onion URL From Script Host
id: c9e7f3a4-2b1d-4f8a-9c3e-5d6a7b8c9e02
description: Detects curl.exe invoked by wscript/cscript/cmd/powershell (or worm-specific ugate.exe) with a Tor SOCKS proxy flag or a .onion URL — the documented screenshot exfiltration channel for the LNK USB clipper.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/usb-worm-spreads-crypto-stealing-malware-via-windows-shortcut-files/
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.t1113
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\curl.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '--socks5'
      - 'socks5h://'
      - '127.0.0.1:9050'
      - '.onion'
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\ugate.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\curl.exe OR *\\CURL.EXE) @CommandLine:(*--socks5* OR *socks5h\:\/\/* OR *127.0.0.1\:9050* OR *.onion*) @ParentImage:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\ugate.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\curl\.exe$/i ParentBaseFileName=/\\(wscript|cscript|cmd|powershell|pwsh|ugate)\.exe$/i | regex("(--socks5|socks5h://|127\.0\.0\.1:9050|\.onion)", field=CommandLine)
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="curl.exe" (Processes.process="*--socks5*" OR Processes.process="*socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050*" OR Processes.process="*.onion*" OR Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:9050*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="curl.exe" (Processes.process="*--socks5*" OR Processes.process="*socks5h://127.0.0.1:9050*" OR Processes.process="*.onion*" OR Processes.process="*127.0.0.1:9050*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Kirby CMS Panel installation endpoint accessed from external IP (CVE-2026-54003) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the Kirby Panel installation URI (/panel/installation) that complete from a non-private source IP. On a production Kirby site with an admin already created, the install endpoint should never be reachable; an external hit indicates either a vulnerable pre-install state being probed or active exploitation of the Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP header-confusion bypass. Rationale: Article specifies the attack target is the Kirby Panel installation flow (canonical URI /panel/installation), exploitable only when the site has no admin yet and the reverse proxy supplies Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP. Any external POST/GET to the install endpoint on a production site is high-fidelity — the endpoint is functionally unreachable post-setup. Private-IP exclusion strips dev/staging noise.
ATT&CKT1190 T1656
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer performing genuine first-time site install from outside the corporate network
  • External vulnerability scanners (Tenable, Qualys, Nuclei) probing /panel/installation as a CVE check
  • Internet-wide opportunistic scanning (Censys/Shodan crawlers) hitting the install URI on a freshly stood-up host
  • Migration or DR rebuild where the site is temporarily admin-less and admin connects from a remote IP
  • Pen-test / red-team reconnaissance against the property
Suppression filter
| where UA !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Nuclei", "masscan", "zgrab", "Censys", "InternetMeasurement") | where ClientIP !in (dynamic(["<known-scanner-IPs>", "<dev-admin-home-IP>"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the Kirby version of the targeted host (vulnerable: <=4.9.3 or 5.0.0-alpha.1 through 5.4.3). Check the HTTP response code — 200 on a POST to /panel/installation means the request was accepted; pair with site/accounts/ inventory to see if a new admin was actually written. Identify the source IP and resolve geo/ASN. Step 2 (contain): If admin creation succeeded, take the site offline, force-delete the rogue account directory under site/accounts/, rotate any secrets the rogue admin could have exfiltrated, and patch to Kirby 4.9.4 or 5.4.4. If only probing, block source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the source IP across all web logs for the prior 30 days — same actor may have probed multiple Kirby properties. Review reverse-proxy config to confirm whether Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP headers are being passed and the upstream Kirby version handles them correctly. Audit all internet-facing Kirby installs for unpatched versions.
// Defender Advanced Hunting has no native web-access-log table; this surfaces the post-install admin login from the host side as a proxy signal
let PanelHosts = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where IsInternetFacing == true
    | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where DeviceId in (PanelHosts)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nginx","nginx.exe","httpd","httpd.exe","apache2","caddy","w3wp.exe","php-fpm","php-fpm.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Primary detection: Kirby Panel install endpoint hit from external IP
let KirbyInstallPaths = dynamic(["/panel/installation", "/panel/install", "/api/users"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csUriStem has_any (KirbyInstallPaths)
  | where csMethod in ("POST","PUT","GET")
  | extend Src="W3CIIS", ClientIP=cIP, URI=csUriStem, Method=csMethod, Status=tostring(scStatus), UA=csUserAgent),
(AppServiceHTTPLogs
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where CsUriStem has_any (KirbyInstallPaths)
  | where CsMethod in ("POST","PUT","GET")
  | extend Src="AppService", ClientIP=CIp, URI=CsUriStem, Method=CsMethod, Status=tostring(ScStatus), UA=UserAgent),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has_any (KirbyInstallPaths)
  | where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT","GET")
  | extend Src="CEF", ClientIP=SourceIP, URI=RequestURL, Method=RequestMethod, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), UA=RequestClientApplication)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(ClientIP)) and ClientIP !startswith "127." and ClientIP != "::1"
| project TimeGenerated, Src, ClientIP, URI, Method, Status, UA
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Kirby CMS admin account file created under site/accounts/ by web server process (CVE-2026-54003) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a new Kirby account file (index.php / .txt / .yml) under the site/accounts/ directory by a web-server runtime process (php-fpm, nginx, apache, w3wp). After initial site setup, Kirby account files are normally added via the authenticated Panel — a new account directory appearing under site/accounts/ outside of a planned admin onboarding indicates either CVE-2026-54003 exploitation or another path to writing account YAML. Rationale: Kill-chain phase 3 explicitly names site/accounts/ as the persistence artefact — Kirby stores account YAML under that directory and the install flow's only side effect is dropping a new admin file there. Constraining the writer to web-server runtime processes (php-fpm, nginx, etc.) eliminates legitimate file-management writes from sysadmins or backup tooling. This is the cleanest exploitation-success signal: it fires only when an account was actually written, not on probe attempts.
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine first-time admin account creation via the Kirby install flow (intended behaviour on freshly-provisioned sites)
  • Migration / backup restore where site/accounts/ is being repopulated from a snapshot
  • Developer using Kirby CLI (kirby command) under the web-server user to programmatically provision accounts
  • Bulk user import via a Kirby plugin run from a web request
  • Configuration management (Ansible / Salt) writing accounts as the web user during deployment
Suppression filter
| where ActorUsername !in ("deployment-bot","backup-svc") | where TargetFilePath !contains "/backup/" and TargetFilePath !contains "/restore/"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the new account YAML — check the role: field (admin is the dangerous case) and the user email. Correlate Timestamp ± 60s against web access logs for POSTs to /panel/installation from the same host to confirm the exploitation path. Verify Kirby version (vulnerable: <=4.9.3 or 5.0.0-alpha.1 through 5.4.3). Step 2 (contain): Delete the rogue account directory under site/accounts/, terminate any active Panel sessions, rotate site secrets and any admin API tokens the rogue account could have minted, then upgrade Kirby to 4.9.4 / 5.4.4. If reverse proxy is upstream, audit its config to ensure Forwarded/X-Client-IP/X-Real-IP are either stripped or trusted appropriately. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the web-server process PID to enumerate every file write in the same session — check site/content/ for tampered pages, site/plugins/ for malicious plugin drops, and /site/config/ for unauthorized config changes. Review subsequent Panel/API auth events for the new account's user ID 
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/site/accounts/", @"\site\accounts\")
| where FileName in~ ("index.php","user.txt","index.yml","index.yaml",".htpasswd") or FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.0","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","php-fpm8.3","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php","nginx","nginx.exe","httpd","httpd.exe","apache2","w3wp.exe","caddy")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/site/accounts/", @"\site\accounts\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("index.php","user.txt","index.yml","index.yaml",".htpasswd") or TargetFileName endswith ".php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php.exe","php-cgi.exe","php","nginx","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe","caddy")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54003")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-54003")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-54003")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-54003")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Critical

Microsoft Details Windows Clipper Malware Campaign Using USB LNK Worm and Tor-Based C2

The Hacker News
2026-06-18 9 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft has disclosed details of a Windows-based cryptocurrency clipper campaign that has targeted users since February 2026 with clipboard-intercepting malware with self-spreading capabilities and using the Tor anonymity network to hide communication. "The clipper in this campaign relies on Windows Script Host and ActiveX-driven logic to launch a bundled Tor proxy and poll a hidden-service C2

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] USB-borne LNK spawns wscript/cscript referencing removable drive path
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] WScript/CScript spawning curl, cmd, or PowerShell (Microsoft-recommended clipper signal) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Scheduled task registers wscript/cscript-launched payload for clipper persistence · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Local SOCKS5 listener on Tor-default port from non-browser binary (bundled Tor proxy) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PowerShell screen capture via System.Drawing CopyFromScreen (Microsoft clipper signal) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
USB-borne LNK spawns wscript/cscript referencing removable drive path AIDelivery High
Hunts the initial-access vector described by Microsoft: a user double-clicks a LNK file on a USB drive that mimics a hidden DOC/XLSX/PDF, causing explorer.exe to launch wscript.exe or cscript.exe with arguments pointing at a removable-drive path. This is the worm's entry point before persistence is installed. Rationale: Article explicitly states the LNK files on USB carry 'arguments that line to the worm component' which the user launches thinking it is a hidden DOC/XLSX/PDF. The parent of a user-clicked LNK is explorer.exe; the child is wscript/cscript; the command line will reference the removable-drive path. Removable-drive letters typically fall in D:-Z: range and combine with .lnk/.vbs/.js extensions for very high fidelity.
ATT&CKT1091 T1204.001 T1059.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate VBS/JS deployment scripts run from network share mapped to drive letters E:/F:
  • IT admin testing autorun behaviour with benign scripts on USB
  • Document-management software auto-launching .vbs file-rename helpers
  • User-installed portable apps on USB drives that ship with .vbs launchers (PortableApps.com)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and identify the script path; check DeviceFileEvents on the source drive letter for hidden DOC/XLSX/PDF files with matching LNK siblings. Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, eject and quarantine the USB device, dump the script body for sandbox analysis. Hunt: query DeviceProcessEvents across the fleet for the same script SHA256 over 30 days, look for scheduled-task creations referencing the same script path, and review DeviceNetworkEvents for any local-loopback SOCKS5 (9050/9150) listeners that may indicate the Tor proxy stage has already deployed.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)[D-Z]:\\"
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".lnk",".vbs",".js",".vbe",".jse")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)[D-Z]:\\" or CommandLine has_any (".lnk",".vbs",".js",".vbe",".jse")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: USB LNK Worm Spawns Windows Script Host from Removable Drive

WScript/CScript spawning curl, cmd, or PowerShell (Microsoft-recommended clipper signal) AIExploitation High
Hunts the execution chain Microsoft explicitly recommended defenders watch for: wscript.exe or cscript.exe launching curl, cmd.exe, PowerShell, or unexpected executables. This is the clipper's ActiveXObject-driven WScript code reaching out to fetch payloads or invoke its bundled Tor proxy. Rationale: Direct quote from Microsoft in the article: defenders should look for 'use of WScript, CScript, or related script engines for launching curl, cmd.exe, PowerShell, or unexpected executables.' The clipper's ActiveXObject design routes everything through WScript, so this parent/child relationship is the canonical execution fingerprint.
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy enterprise VBScript admin tooling that shells out to PowerShell for system queries
  • SCCM/Intune deployment wrappers that chain VBS to cmd.exe for legacy installer logic
  • Citrix logon scripts invoking certutil for cert pinning
  • Internal IT helpdesk scripts using cscript-driven cmd.exe wrappers
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\System32\\CCM\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Microsoft Intune Management Extension\\"
Response runbook
Triage: extract the parent script path and full ChildCmd; pull the script content from disk (if still present) for sandbox analysis. Contain: kill the parent script process tree, isolate the host, and block the script SHA256 via Defender custom IOC. Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents for the parent script process making outbound connections to .onion-style infrastructure or to localhost SOCKS5 ports (9050/9150), and look for AsepValueUpdate registry persistence written by the same wscript/cscript instance.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","wget.exe","mshta.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentScript = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentFolder = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ChildProcess = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("curl.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","wget.exe","mshta.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Scheduled task registers wscript/cscript-launched payload for clipper persistence AIInstallation High
Detects the worm component installing scheduled-task persistence for itself and the clipper, as described in the article. Looks for schtasks.exe creating tasks whose action invokes wscript.exe or cscript.exe with a user-writable path (Temp, AppData, ProgramData, Public). Rationale: Article: 'The worm component … deploys scheduled tasks as a form of persistence for both the worm component and the stealer component.' The clipper uses WScript/ActiveXObject so any installed task action will reference wscript or cscript pointing at a payload outside Program Files — that combination is rarely benign.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise login-banner script deployed via scheduled task pointing to ProgramData
  • Software-vendor uninstaller cleanup tasks shipping VBS in %ProgramData%\<Vendor>\
  • Adobe/Java updater registered as scheduled-task VBS hooks
  • IT-admin ad-hoc tasks running diagnostic VBS from a user profile path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\System32\\CCM\\" and ProcessCommandLine !has "\\Program Files\\"
Response runbook
Triage: extract task name and the full TR (task-run) argument from the command line; pull the referenced script for sandbox analysis. Contain: delete the scheduled task with schtasks /Delete /F, kill any running instances, and isolate the host. Hunt: query DeviceEvents for ActionType=ScheduledTaskCreated across the fleet for the same script SHA256 or task name, and check DeviceFileEvents for the original payload file to identify the delivery vector (USB drive letter or download URL).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/CREATE")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Public\\","\\Users\\Public\\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          Parent = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/Create","/CREATE")
| where CommandLine has_any ("wscript","cscript")
| where CommandLine has_any ("\\AppData\\","\\Temp\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Public\\","\\Users\\Public\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Schtasks Registers WScript Or CScript Payload From User-Writable Path
id: 5f2b9c41-7d18-4a93-91be-3e95ad6c4d22
description: Detects schtasks.exe creating a scheduled task whose action invokes wscript.exe or cscript.exe against a payload in a user-writable directory, matching the Microsoft-reported clipper persistence step.

Local SOCKS5 listener on Tor-default port from non-browser binary (bundled Tor proxy) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the bundled Tor client described in the article: a renamed Tor binary opening a local SOCKS5 listener on the default Tor ports (9050/9150) from a process that is not Tor Browser, Brave, or another known Tor-aware app. The clipper routes C2 through this local proxy, so the listener is a strong signal. Rationale: Article states the malware 'launches a renamed Tor binary in a hidden window' and 'routes traffic through a local SOCKS5 proxy.' Tor's default SOCKS5 ports are 9050 (tor.exe) and 9150 (Tor Browser). A loopback connection or listener on those ports from a process that is NOT a known Tor client is exactly the renamed-Tor signature the article describes.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1572 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using Tor SOCKS proxy via a custom Python script for legitimate research
  • Privacy-tool users running Tor via OnionShare or BridgeRelay portables under a renamed wrapper
  • Penetration-tester using torsocks during an authorised engagement
  • Anonymisation-aware crypto wallet apps (e.g. Wasabi, Samourai) that ship their own SOCKS5 binding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\Tor Browser\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\OnionShare\\"
Response runbook
Triage: identify the binding process via InitiatingProcessSHA256 and InitiatingProcessFolderPath; submit hash to threat intel and inspect the on-disk binary for Tor strings/imports despite the renamed filename. Contain: kill the proxy process, isolate the host, capture memory if possible, then quarantine the binary. Hunt: query DeviceProcessEvents for the same SHA256 across the fleet, check DeviceRegistryEvents and scheduled-task creations referencing the same path, and look at DeviceFileEvents for any .onion-related config files (torrc) dropped to %AppData% or %ProgramData%.
let TorPorts = dynamic([9050, 9150]);
let KnownTorClients = dynamic(["tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe","brave.exe","torbrowser.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where RemotePort in (TorPorts) or LocalPort in (TorPorts)
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or LocalIP in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (KnownTorClients)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256,
          LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let TorPorts = dynamic([9050, 9150]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber in (TorPorts) or SrcPortNumber in (TorPorts)
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1") or SrcIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcPortNumber, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationPort:9050 OR @DestinationPort:9150) @DestinationIp:(127.0.0.1 OR \:\:1) -@Image:(*\\tor.exe OR *\\Tor.exe OR *\\TOR.EXE OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\Firefox.exe OR *\\tor-browser.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\Brave.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=9050 OR RemotePort=9150) RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\./
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(tor|firefox|tor-browser|torbrowser|brave)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port=9050 OR All_Traffic.dest_port=9150) (All_Traffic.dest_ip="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="::1") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where NOT (process_name IN ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe","brave.exe"))
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_port=9050 OR All_Traffic.dest_port=9150) (All_Traffic.dest_ip="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest_ip="::1") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where NOT (process_name IN ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe","brave.exe"))
PowerShell screen capture via System.Drawing CopyFromScreen (Microsoft clipper signal) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the clipper's screenshot-exfiltration stage. Microsoft's article explicitly recommends 'PowerShell-based screen capture' detection. The Bitmap/Graphics/CopyFromScreen API pattern is the canonical way PowerShell grabs the desktop and is rarely seen in benign workloads. Rationale: Direct Microsoft recommendation in the article: 'defenders prioritize behavioral detections … specifically looking for PowerShell-based screen capture.' The .NET System.Drawing classes with CopyFromScreen are the standard PowerShell screenshot pattern and the clipper does periodic screen-grab exfiltration over Tor — so the API string is the natural cmd-line fingerprint.
ATT&CKT1113 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal ITAM or RMM tool grabbing screenshots for endpoint inventory dashboards
  • Developer testing a screenshot-utility PowerShell module
  • Help-desk session-recording scripts using Bitmap APIs for incident capture
  • ScreenConnect/ConnectWise remote-support agents using PowerShell wrappers for thumbnails
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\ScreenConnect\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\ConnectWise\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\SCCM\\"
Response runbook
Triage: extract the full PowerShell command line, decode any inline base64 or compressed payload, identify the target output path (where the bitmap is written). Contain: kill the PowerShell process tree, isolate the host, and review %TEMP%/%APPDATA% for recently-written PNG/JPG/BMP files that may be queued for Tor upload. Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName — if wscript.exe or cscript.exe is the parent, this is the clipper chain; query DeviceNetworkEvents for the parent process touching localhost:9050/9150 and pull any scheduled tasks that launch the same script.
DeviceProcessEvents

praisonai-platform admin DELETE on /workspaces or /{workspace}/members endpoints AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts DELETE requests against praisonai-platform's owner-gated routes (DELETE /workspaces/{uuid} and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}). A successful (2xx) DELETE without an upstream auth challenge in a vulnerable 0.1.4 deployment is the post-forgery action the attacker uses to wipe a workspace or evict members. Pivots on the article's exact URL shapes. Rationale: URL templates are taken verbatim from the article (DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}). UUIDv4 in path constrains FPs, 2xx narrows to actions that actually executed. We don't try to validate the JWT signature in the SIEM — we surface the outcome of the bypass primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c2m8-4gcg-v22g • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h8q5-cp56-rr65
ATT&CKT1190 T1485 T1531
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workspace owner deleting their own workspace from the UI
  • Automated tenant-lifecycle/cleanup cron job calling DELETE /workspaces/{id} with a properly issued JWT
  • Member self-removal where a co-member deletes themselves via the UI
  • Integration / E2E test suites running against a staging instance
  • QA load tests that create-then-delete workspaces
Suppression filter
| where User == "" or User == "-" or isempty(User) or UserAgent !has_any ("praisonai-cli", "praisonai-ui", "jobs-runner")
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: pull the raw request, decode the bearer JWT, and check the `iss`/`kid` and signature. If HS256 signed with `dev-secret-change-me` (the literal from auth_service.py:25), this is exploitation, not abuse. Cross-check the source IP against the workspace owner's recent legitimate sessions and the user-agent against the platform's known clients. Step 2 — contain: rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET to a strong random value and restart the praisonai-platform process so the module-load guard re-evaluates; invalidate all outstanding sessions; if data was deleted, fail over to backup and restrict the offending source IP at the WAF. Step 3 — hunt: pull all DELETE/PATCH/PUT traffic from that IP and any IP that issued requests with the same forged JWT `sub` over the last 30d; pivot on prior GET /{workspace_id}/members calls (the article's documented enumeration step) from the same client.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
union isfuzzy=true
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where HttpMethod == "DELETE"
  | where Url matches regex @"/workspaces/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?$"
      or Url matches regex @"/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/members/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?$"
  | where HttpStatusCode between (200 .. 299)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, User = SrcUsername, Method = HttpMethod, Path = Url, Status = HttpStatusCode, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, AuthHeaderLen = strlen(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization), Source = "ImWebSession"),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where RequestMethod == "DELETE"
  | where RequestURL matches regex @"/workspaces/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?$"
      or RequestURL matches regex @"/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/members/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?$"
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = DestinationHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, User = SourceUserName, Method = RequestMethod, Path = RequestURL, Status = tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent = RequestClientApplication, AuthHeaderLen = int(null), Source = "CommonSecurityLog"),
(W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where csMethod == "DELETE"
  | where csUriStem matches regex @"/workspaces/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?$"
      or csUriStem matches regex @"/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/members/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?$"
  | where scStatus between (200 .. 299)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP = cIP, User = csUserName, Method = csMethod, Path = csUriStem, Status = tostring(scStatus), UserAgent = csUserAgent, AuthHeaderLen = int(null), Source = "W3CIISLog")
| extend WorkspaceId = coalesce(extract(@"/workspaces/([0-9a-fA-F-]{36})", 1, Path), extract(@"/([0-9a-fA-F-]{36})/members/", 1, Path))
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: praisonai-platform Owner-Gated DELETE on Workspace or Member Endpoint
id: 7f9c2e1b-4a5d-4ba8-9c3e-2f8b1a6d0e94
status: experimental
description: Detects DELETE requests against praisonai-platform's require_workspace_owner-gated routes (DELETE /workspaces/{uuid} and DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}). Under the GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq JWT-secret default ("dev-secret-change-me"), a forged token reaches these destructive endpoints.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f38v-77qj-h4jq
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/19
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1485
  - attack.t1531
  - attack.impact
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method: DELETE
  selection_url:
    cs-uri-stem|re: '^(/workspaces/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?|/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/members/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?)$'
  selection_status:
    sc-status:
      - 200
      - 204
  condition: selection_method and selection_url and selection_status
falsepositives:
  - Workspace-owner-initiated cleanup from the application UI
  - Automated tenant-lifecycle jobs run with a real (non-default) PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET
level: high
(source:python OR source:nginx OR source:fastapi) @http.method:DELETE (@http.url_details.path:/workspaces/* OR @http.url_details.path:*/members/*) @http.status_code:[200 TO 299]

praisonai-platform attack chain: member enumeration GET followed by workspace-delete AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the article's documented two-step takeover: GET /{workspace_id}/members (to read the owner's user_id for forging the sub) followed within a short window by DELETE /workspaces/{workspace_id} or DELETE /{workspace_id}/members/{user_id} on the SAME workspace from the same client. Materially higher fidelity than either step alone. Rationale: The article explicitly walks the attack: read GET /{workspace_id}/members to learn the owner's user_id, mint a JWT with that sub via the public default secret, then call require_workspace_owner-gated DELETE routes. The temporal-correlation join on workspace_id is the high-fidelity pivot — single-IP enum-then-destroy on the same workspace in 30m is the article's reproduction sequence verbatim. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3qg8-5g3r-79v5 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c2m8-4gcg-v22g • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h8q5-cp56-rr65
ATT&CKT1190 T1087 T1485 T1531
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Workspace owner cleaning up members then deleting an obsolete workspace from the same UI session
  • Admin offboarding tool: list members → remove each → delete workspace, all via a properly issued service-account JWT
  • E2E test suite that provisions a workspace, enumerates, then tears down
  • Migration script that lists members per workspace for export then deletes source workspaces post-migration
Suppression filter
| where DestructClientIP == EnumClientIP and DelaySeconds <= 1800 | where DestructUA !has_any ("praisonai-admin-cli", "tenant-lifecycle-job", "e2e-runner")
Response runbook
Step 1 — triage: pull both the enum (GET /members) and destroy (DELETE) request rows for the matched WorkspaceId. Decode the bearer JWT used in the DELETE request: if HS256 with the `dev-secret-change-me` literal, confirmed exploitation. Note the `sub` claim — that's the user being impersonated. Step 2 — contain: rotate PLATFORM_JWT_SECRET to a 256-bit random value, restart praisonai-platform so the module-load guard re-evaluates, invalidate sessions, and restore the deleted workspace from backup. WAF-block the source IP if it's not a known internal CIDR. Step 3 — hunt: search all GETs on /members from that source IP across the last 30d — those are pre-attack reconnaissance against other workspaces. Pivot on any JWT `sub` claim observed under the default secret and audit every action the impersonated identity took since the vulnerable version was deployed.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMinutes = 30m;
let WebReq = union isfuzzy=true
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, User = SrcUsername, Method = HttpMethod, Path = Url, Status = HttpStatusCode, UA = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DestinationHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, User = SourceUserName, Method = RequestMethod, Path = RequestURL, Status = toint(EventOutcome), UA = RequestClientApplication),
  (W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, ClientIP = cIP, User = csUserName, Method = csMethod, Path = csUriStem, Status = scStatus, UA = csUserAgent);
let Enum = WebReq
  | where Method == "GET"
  | where Path matches regex @"^/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/members/?$"
  | where Status between (200 .. 299)
  | extend WorkspaceId = extract(@"^/([0-9a-fA-F-]{36})/members", 1, Path)
  | project EnumTime = TimeGenerated, EnumClientIP = ClientIP, EnumUser = User, EnumUA = UA, EnumHost = Host, WorkspaceId;
let Destruct = WebReq
  | where Method == "DELETE"
  | where Path matches regex @"^/workspaces/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?$"
      or Path matches regex @"^/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/members/[0-9a-fA-F-]{36}/?$"
  | extend WorkspaceId = coalesce(extract(@"/workspaces/([0-9a-fA-F-]{36})", 1, Path), extract(@"^/([0-9a-fA-F-]{36})/members/", 1, Path))
  | project DestructTime = TimeGenerated, DestructClientIP = ClientIP, DestructUser = User, DestructUA = UA, DestructHost = Host, DestructPath = Path, WorkspaceId;
Enum
| join kind=inner Destruct on WorkspaceId
| where DestructTime between (EnumTime .. EnumTime + WindowMinutes)
| extend DelaySeconds = datetime_diff('second', DestructTime, EnumTime)
| project EnumTime, DestructTime, DelaySeconds, WorkspaceId, EnumClientIP, DestructClientIP, EnumUser, DestructUser, DestructPath, EnumHost, DestructHost, EnumUA, DestructUA
| order by DestructTime desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PraisonAI multiedit tool reading sensitive credentials (GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47)
PraisonAI multiedit tool reading sensitive credentials (GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Python processes running PraisonAI (module 'praisonai.tools.multiedit') accessing files outside any reasonable workspace boundary — SSH private keys, AWS credentials, .env files, /etc/shadow. The multiedit tool's lack of path validation lets prompt-injected agents read arbitrary files via the dry_run diff output or direct read path. Rationale: Detection anchors on three article-specific tokens: (1) Python interpreter as initiating process, (2) 'praisonai' or 'multiedit' in command line (the vulnerable tool's module path is praisonai.tools.multiedit), (3) sensitive credential paths explicitly named in the article's Impact section (/etc/shadow, ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.aws/credentials, .env). The combination is high-fidelity because no legitimate workspace-scoped agent should be traversing to /etc/ or user home credential stores.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer explicitly asking PraisonAI agent to read or rotate their own ~/.aws/credentials in a personal lab environment
  • Legitimate PraisonAI workflow that ingests a project's .env file from inside the workspace (path will contain workspace root, not /root or $HOME)
  • Security researcher reproducing the GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 PoC in a sandbox after the advisory landed
  • PraisonAI agent indexing a Git repository whose path happens to contain '.env.example' or similar template files
  • Automated dotfile sync tool spawned as a child of a PraisonAI orchestration session
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "/workspace/" or FolderPath has "/app/data/")
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "pytest" and FolderPath has "/tests/fixtures/")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the deployment shape — CLI dev workstation vs chatbot integration (Telegram/Discord/Slack with auto_approve_tools=True is the high-risk path). Pull the agent's prompt/conversation log around the file-access timestamp; the prompt that drove the multiedit call is the smoking gun. Step 2 (contain): If the file accessed was a credential store, immediately rotate the secret (SSH key, AWS access key, .env API keys) and revoke active sessions. Pin or remove the multiedit tool from the agent's tool registry until upgraded to praisonai >= 4.6.61. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host for (a) outbound network connections from the Python process to non-corporate destinations in the 10 minutes following the read, (b) subsequent file WRITES by the same process to authorized_keys/.bashrc (see persistence UC), (c) other LLM agent tools in the org's stack with similar path-validation gaps.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
   or ActionType startswith "File"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe", "python3", "python", "python3.exe", "pythonw.exe", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\", @"\.env", @"\.netrc", "/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "/.ssh/", "/.aws/", "/root/", "id_rsa", "id_ed25519", "credentials")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "pythonw")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.ssh/", "/.aws/", "/.env", "/.netrc", "/etc/shadow", "/etc/passwd", "id_rsa", "id_ed25519", "credentials", @"\.ssh\", @"\.aws\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PraisonAI MultiEdit Tool Accessing Sensitive Credentials
id: 8b3f4e2a-91c7-4a5d-b8f1-3e9c5d2a7f64
description: Detects the PraisonAI Python agent (vulnerable multiedit tool, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) reading credentials, SSH keys, or cloud secrets outside any plausible workspace. The multiedit tool lacks path validation and traversal protection.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1552.004
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|contains: 'python'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'praisonai'
      - 'multiedit'
  selection_target:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/.ssh/id_'
      - '/.aws/credentials'
      - '/.aws/config'
      - '/.env'
      - '/.netrc'
      - '/etc/shadow'
      - '/etc/passwd'
      - 'authorized_keys'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_target
falsepositives:
  - Developer explicitly invoking PraisonAI to manage their own credentials/SSH keys
  - Automated PraisonAI workflows that legitimately read .env config from a known workspace
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) @process.name:(python OR python3 OR pythonw) @process.command_line:(*praisonai* OR *multiedit*) @file.path:(*/.ssh/id_* OR */.aws/credentials* OR */.env OR */.netrc OR /etc/shadow OR /etc/passwd OR *authorized_keys*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| ContextImageFileName=/python[3]?(w)?(\.exe)?$/i
| regex("(/\.ssh/id_|/\.aws/credentials|/\.aws/config|/\.env$|/\.netrc|/etc/shadow|/etc/passwd|authorized_keys|\\\\\.ssh\\\\|\\\\\.aws\\\\)", field=TargetFileName)
| join({
    #event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
    | regex("(praisonai|multiedit)", field=CommandLine)
  }, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[CommandLine, ImageFileName])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

PraisonAI multiedit writing to persistence locations (authorized_keys / shell rc / cron) AIInstallation High
Hunts the write-side abuse of the GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47 multiedit vulnerability — a Python PraisonAI process writing/modifying files in canonical Linux/Windows persistence locations (~/.ssh/authorized_keys, ~/.bashrc, ~/.bash_profile, ~/.profile, cron, autostart) where no workspace-scoped agent should ever touch. The advisory explicitly calls out writing to ~/.bashrc and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as the privilege-escalation impact. Rationale: Anchors on the article's Impact section, which explicitly names ~/.bashrc and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as the privilege-escalation outcomes. Combining the Python+praisonai/multiedit cmdline filter with these specific persistence paths makes this alerting-tier — there is essentially no legitimate scenario where a PraisonAI agent should rewrite a user's shell rc or SSH authorized_keys outside an explicit provisioning playbook.
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1546.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using PraisonAI as a deliberate Ansible-style provisioner to push authorized_keys to fleet hosts
  • Developer asking PraisonAI to add an alias to their own .bashrc on a personal dev VM
  • Container/cloud-init bootstrap script that happens to embed PraisonAI for initial host config
  • Security researcher reproducing the PoC from the advisory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "ansible" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "cloud-init")
| where not (DeviceName startswith "dev-" and AccountName == "developer")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Diff the modified file against backup/git history — the inserted content is the payload. Common shapes: a new SSH public key not matching any known engineer fingerprint, a curl|sh trampoline appended to .bashrc, an entry in cron.d calling out to an external URL. Pull the PraisonAI session/prompt that drove the write. Step 2 (contain): Revert the file from backup; if authorized_keys was modified, kill all live SSH sessions for that account and rotate any other access. Disable the agent integration (Telegram/Discord/Slack bot token, API key) and pin praisonai package to >= 4.6.61 across the fleet. Step 3 (hunt): Search 24h forward for SSH logins to this host from any IP whose pubkey matches the freshly-added one; search the org for other hosts where the same praisonai process wrote anywhere outside its workspace.

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe", "python3", "python", "python3.exe", "pythonw.exe", "python3.10", "python3.11", "python3.12")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.ssh/authorized_keys", "/.bashrc", "/.bash_profile", "/.profile", "/.zshrc", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/crontab", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/sudoers", @"\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\")
   or FileName in~ ("authorized_keys", ".bashrc", ".bash_profile", ".profile", ".zshrc", "crontab", "sudoers")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          PreviousFileName, PreviousFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python", "python3", "pythonw")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "multiedit")

   or TargetFileName in~ ("authorized_keys", ".bashrc", ".bash_profile", ".profile", ".zshrc", "crontab", "sudoers")

          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects PraisonAI Python agent (vulnerable multiedit tool, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) writing to authorized_keys, shell rc files, cron, or sudoers - the persistence vectors explicitly called out in the advisory's Impact section.
references:

level: critical

| join({

Vulnerable PraisonAI package exposure (< 4.6.61, GHSA-29w3-p9w9-wc47) AIReconnaissance High
Surfaces hosts running a vulnerable version of the pip:praisonai package so the SOC can drive remediation before exploitation. Pure exposure-management pivot — pairs with the credential-read and persistence detections above so any prior exploitation can be retrospectively hunted on confirmed-vulnerable hosts. Rationale: Targets the exact pip package + version range named in the advisory ('Affected packages: pip:praisonai (vuln < 4.6.61)'). This is the SOC's 'are we even exposed?' query — without it, the hunting detections above have no priority ordering for which hosts to investigate first.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped lab hosts where the vulnerable version is intentionally pinned for reproduction research
  • Hosts where Defender TVM has not yet inventoried pip packages (TVM coverage of Python packages is partial — absence does not mean clean)
  • Containers where the praisonai package lives inside an image that TVM cannot introspect
  • Pre-production hosts scheduled for teardown that won't be patched
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Prioritize the result set by IsInternetFacing == true and by chatbot deployment hosts (Telegram/Discord/Slack-integrated PraisonAI is the high-blast-radius shape per the advisory). Step 2 (contain): Drive upgrade to praisonai >= 4.6.61 via the org's pip/Poetry/uv channel; for hosts that can't upgrade immediately, set auto_approve_tools=False on any chatbot integration and remove multiedit from the agent's tool registry. Step 3 (hunt): For every host this query returns, retro-run the credential-read and persistence UCs over the last 90 days — if praisonai was vulnerable, any historical file-access to /etc/shadow or write to authorized_keys by that python process is high-priority IR work, not noise.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai" or SoftwareName == "praisonai"
| extend VersionParts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(VersionParts[0]), Minor = toint(VersionParts[1]), Patch = toint(VersionParts[2])
| where Major < 4
   or (Major == 4 and Minor < 6)
   or (Major == 4 and Minor == 6 and Patch < 61)
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceInfo
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId
    | project DeviceId, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup, LoggedOnUsers
  ) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion,
          OSPlatform, IsInternetFacing, MachineGroup, LoggedOnUsers
| order by tostring(IsInternetFacing) desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai"
| extend VersionParts = split(SoftwareVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(VersionParts[0]), Minor = toint(VersionParts[1]), Patch = toint(VersionParts[2])
| where Major < 4
   or (Major == 4 and Minor < 6)
   or (Major == 4 and Minor == 6 and Patch < 61)
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel
| order by DeviceName asc

Unauthenticated JSON-RPC tools/call hitting an internal MCP HTTP listener AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST traffic carrying JSON-RPC method strings ('tools/call','tools/list','resources/read','prompts/get') against the MCP server's default listener port. Targets the specific exploit shape from GHSA-j4f3-55x4-r6q2 where the praisonai TypeScript MCPServer accepts these methods with no Authorization check and binds to all interfaces. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two strongest fingerprints: (1) the specific JSON-RPC method strings handleRequest() dispatches without auth ('tools/call','tools/list','resources/read','prompts/get','initialize'), and (2) the default port 3000 + node.exe parent process running praisonai/mcp/server code. The Sentinel query also captures the article's PoV confirming 'Bearer invalid' is ignored — a Bearer-invalid POST that returns 200 is decisive.
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal MCP clients on the same host invoking tools/list against a development instance
  • Security scanners (Nuclei, Burp, internal pentest) probing JSON-RPC endpoints on port 3000
  • Loopback PoV/PoC runs by the developer hardening their MCP server
  • Other JSON-RPC services on port 3000 unrelated to praisonai (e.g. Ethereum-style RPC, internal dashboards)
  • Health-check / monitoring probes that send empty POST bodies
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("--test", "--scan", "NODE_ENV=development") | where RemoteIP !in (vuln_scanner_ips) | where AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the offending host's praisonai version (`npm ls praisonai`) and confirm MCPServer.start() is called with HTTP transport; review the WAF/proxy log around the alert window for the source IP, JSON-RPC method, and whether Authorization header was present/valid. Step 2 (contain): if the listener is reachable from outside the trust boundary, block inbound 3000 at the host firewall, restart the node process bound to 127.0.0.1, or stop the service until a patched version (post-1.7.1 with auth wired) is deployed. Step 3 (hunt): for the same source IP, search EmailEvents and DeviceProcessEvents for follow-on activity — node.exe spawning cmd/powershell/bash (tool handler abuse), unexpected file writes by node.exe, and DNS/outbound from the node process to non-corp domains within 1 hour of the inbound JSON-RPC.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 3000
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "mcp/server", "MCPServer")
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback", "Private") or RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, LocalIP, LocalPort,
          InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 3000
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where Message has_any ('"method":"tools/call"', '"method":"tools/list"', '"method":"resources/read"', '"method":"prompts/get"', '"method":"initialize"')
| extend AuthHeaderPresent = Message has "Authorization:"
| extend AuthInvalid = Message has_cs "Authorization: Bearer invalid" or Message matches regex @"(?i)Authorization:\s*Bearer\s+(invalid|test|null|undefined)\b"
| where not(AuthHeaderPresent) or AuthInvalid
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, AuthHeaderPresent, AuthInvalid, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable praisonai npm package (<=1.7.1) installed on host AIWeaponization High
Detects the on-disk fingerprint of the vulnerable npm package (`node_modules/praisonai/package.json` and the unguarded `src/praisonai-ts/src/mcp/server.ts` file) being written during `npm install`. Treat as a hunting hook to find every machine that needs patching before the wider attack-surface hunt. Rationale: Targets the exact file artefacts named in the article ('src/praisonai-ts/src/mcp/server.ts' and the npm package layout). Combining 'node_modules/praisonai' with an npm/yarn/pnpm parent eliminates source-checkout false positives. Pairs with UC1 — patch the hosts this lights up before UC1 trips for real.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer machines doing legitimate development against the praisonai source tree (not exposed to network)
  • CI build runners installing dependencies in ephemeral containers for testing
  • Security-research/sandbox VMs deliberately installing the vulnerable version for reproduction
  • Mirror/cache servers (Verdaccio, Artifactory) pre-fetching the package
  • Old development branches resurrected during git checkout that contain the package.json on disk but never serve it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Users\\" | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\" | where DeviceName !in (dev_workstations_watchlist)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): for each host, capture `node_modules/praisonai/package.json` `version` and `dependencies`; confirm whether the host runs `MCPServer.start({port:...})` in production code (grep repo for `MCPServer` instantiation). Step 2 (contain): if production, force-upgrade to a patched version once published or pin to a fork that wires MCPSecurity into startHttp() and binds to 127.0.0.1; in the interim, add a host-firewall rule blocking inbound 3000 from non-loopback. Step 3 (hunt): for every host that has the file, pivot to UC1 over the last 30 days to check whether anyone has already exploited it; pull `node.exe` outbound DNS and process-tree for the same window.

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "node_modules\\praisonai" or FolderPath has "node_modules/praisonai" or FolderPath has "praisonai-ts\\src\\mcp" or FolderPath has "praisonai-ts/src/mcp"
| where FileName in~ ("package.json", "server.ts", "server.js")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe", "npm-cli.js", "node.exe", "pnpm.exe", "yarn.exe", "corepack.exe")

| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules/praisonai" or TargetFilePath has "node_modules\\praisonai" or TargetFilePath has "praisonai-ts/src/mcp" or TargetFilePath has "praisonai-ts\\src\\mcp"

Node.js praisonai MCP server spawning shell or scripting interpreter (tool-call abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Post-exploitation pivot: an unauthenticated tools/call from UC1 lets the attacker invoke whatever tool handlers the MCPServer registered. Many handlers wrap shell, file, or db actions. This catches node.exe (with praisonai in its cmdline) spawning cmd/powershell/bash/sh as a child — the most common abuse shape regardless of which specific tool is registered. Rationale: The article notes 'MCP tools commonly wrap filesystem operations, API clients, database queries, agent actions, deployment operations, email/Slack actions, browser automation, and code execution'. A node.exe parent whose cmdline references praisonai/MCPServer spawning a shell or scripting interpreter is the single highest-fidelity post-exploit signature regardless of which tool was registered, and pairs cleanly with UC1 as the network-side trigger.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate registered MCP tools that genuinely wrap shell commands (e.g. a 'run_terminal' tool) used by the application's own AI agent loop
  • Developer testing the MCPServer locally with example tools that exec shell
  • npm postinstall scripts running during package upgrade (node spawning shell briefly)
  • CI/CD pipelines using praisonai for build-step orchestration that legitimately spawn shells
  • Application healthcheck/monitoring scripts invoked by node parent
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has_any ("npm install", "npm run", "node-gyp", "yarn install") | where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("npm.exe", "yarn.exe", "pnpm.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): grab the child process commandline, hash, and any spawned descendants — confirm whether the action looks like a registered MCP tool's legitimate work or arbitrary attacker input (recon strings, encoded payloads, outbound network from the child). Pull the inbound JSON-RPC request from UC1 in the same minute. Step 2 (contain): isolate the host (or stop the node MCP service), revoke any credentials accessible to the node process (env vars, IAM role, .aws/credentials, .npmrc tokens). Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the child's outbound DNS/IPs and any file writes for next-stage payloads; check the source IP of the UC1 request against threat intel and enumerate every other host running praisonai (UC2) for the same source-IP probes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "MCPServer", "mcp/server", "mcp\\server")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash.exe", "wsl.exe", "sh.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "node" or ParentProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai", "praisonai-ts", "MCPServer", "mcp/server", "mcp\\server")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "bash", "sh", "wsl.exe", "wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "curl.exe", "certutil.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
